Semiparametric causal mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials with post-treatment confounding

Daeyoung Ham1, Chao Cheng2, and Fan Li3,4 1Department of Statistics and Data Science, University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA 2Department of Statistics and Data Science, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, MO, USA 3Department of Biostatistics, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, USA 4Center for Methods in Implementation and Prevention Science, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT, USA daeyoung.ham@utsa.edu; chaoc@wustl.edu; fan.f.li@yale.edu
Abstract

Causal mediation analysis of cluster-randomized trials can reveal how interventions affect outcomes through individual and spillover pathways. Most existing methods target natural mediation effects under assumptions that exclude treatment-induced mediator–outcome confounding. We develop a semiparametric framework for interventional mediation effects that accommodates such confounding and within-cluster interference without requiring cross-world independence assumptions. We identify cluster-average and individual-average direct and indirect effects and decompose the indirect effect into individual and spillover components, distinguishing pathways through an individual’s own mediator and those of other cluster members. These contrasts evaluate hypothetical interventions on the joint mediator distribution and can differ from treatment effects carried through individual causal pathways represented by natural effects, thereby providing an intervention-oriented perspective that complements natural effects. We derive efficient influence functions to construct estimators using cluster-level cross-fitting, characterize their multiple-robustness properties, and establish conditions for asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency. To facilitate implementation, we develop a lower-dimensional reparameterization that reduces the need for multivariate density estimation and integration and allows nuisance functions to be estimated using parametric models or machine learning. Simulation studies evaluate finite-sample performance, and an application to a cluster-randomized trial of cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain illustrates the proposed methods.

Keywords: Cluster-randomized trials; Efficient influence functions; Interventional mediation; Post-treatment confounding; Within-cluster interference.

1 Introduction

Cluster-randomized trials, in which groups of individuals rather than individual participants are randomized to treatment conditions, are widely used to evaluate interventions in health, biomedical, and social science research. The primary analysis of a cluster-randomized trial typically assesses whether an intervention is effective by estimating its total effect on a final outcome (Hayes and Moulton, 2017; Li et al., 2025). The total effect alone, however, does not reveal the mechanisms through which the intervention operates. Causal mediation analysis complements this overall assessment by examining pathways through post-treatment intermediate variables, referred to as mediators (Imai et al., 2010). By distinguishing indirect effects operating through the mediator from direct effects operating through other pathways, causal mediation analysis can deepen our understanding of how an intervention works and inform the design and refinement of future interventions.

A growing literature has investigated causal mechanisms in cluster-randomized trials. Relative to simpler individually randomized trials, mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials is further complicated by within-cluster interference, under which one individual’s mediator may affect not only that individual’s own outcome but also the outcomes of other members of the same cluster. In the single-mediator setting, VanderWeele et al. (2013) decomposed the natural indirect effect into an individual mediation effect, capturing pathways through an individual’s own mediator, and a spillover mediation effect, capturing pathways through the mediators of other individuals in the same cluster. Cheng and Li (2026) established semiparametric efficiency theory for inferring these effect estimands and developed efficient estimators that accommodate data-adaptive machine-learning methods for nuisance modeling. Subsequent work has extended this literature to settings with multiple mediators. For two unordered mediators, Ohnishi and Li (2026) decomposed the mediator-specific exit indirect effect (Xia and Chan, 2022) into exit individual and exit spillover mediation effects, thereby providing a finer characterization of individual and spillover pathways, and developed a Bayesian nonparametric approach for estimation and inference. Tong et al. (2026) generalized these exit mediation effects to an arbitrary number of mediators without requiring a known causal ordering among them and constructed efficient debiased machine-learning estimators. Together, these developments have substantially expanded the range of causal mechanisms that can be studied in cluster-randomized trials. Existing methods, however, mostly focus on settings without treatment-induced confounding of the mediator–outcome relationship.

Treatment-induced mediator-outcome confounding arises when the treatment affects an intermediate post-treatment variable that, in turn, influences both the mediator and the outcome. In this setting, natural mediation effects are generally not identified under sequential ignorability assumptions, and identifying them requires additional unverifiable restrictions on counterfactual quantities (Avin et al., 2005; Tchetgen Tchetgen and VanderWeele, 2014; Xia and Chan, 2023). One approach to this problem is to target the natural mediation effects and assess their sensitivity to the unidentified cross-world dependence between the potential mediator and the potential outcome. For example, Ohnishi et al. (2025) developed a Bayesian sensitivity analysis framework for natural mediation effects in cluster-randomized trials subject to post-treatment confounding, using a Gaussian copula model to parameterize the residual dependence between counterfactual mediator and outcome under different treatment conditions. As a complementary approach, we target interventional analogues of natural mediation effects, which replace individual-specific natural mediator values with stochastic draws from treatment-specific mediator distributions (Petersen et al., 2006; VanderWeele et al., 2014; Vansteelandt and Daniel, 2017). In the independent data setting, these effects can be identified in the presence of observed treatment-induced mediator-outcome confounding under appropriate exchangeability and positivity conditions, without specifying the unidentified cross-world dependence required for natural effects (Díaz et al., 2021; Hejazi et al., 2023). In cluster-randomized trials, an individual’s outcome may depend on both their own mediator and those of other cluster members, motivating interventions on the joint mediator distribution to assess how changes in marginal distributions and their dependence affect the outcomes. The resulting contrasts quantifies the potential value of hypothetical mediator interventions by comparing mean outcomes under treatment and control mediator distributions while holding treatment fixed, and can differ from the treatment effects carried through individual causal pathways that natural effects explain (Miles, 2023). Interventional effects provide a complementary, intervention-oriented perspective on the role of mediators.

We seek to develop novel semiparametric methods for interventional mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials with treatment-induced mediator-outcome confounding. Our contributions are threefold. First, we define interventional direct and indirect effects by drawing the within-cluster mediator vector from its treatment-specific distribution conditional on baseline information, and further decompose the interventional indirect effect into individual and spillover components operating through an individual’s own mediator and the mediators of other cluster members, respectively. The proposed estimands allow arbitrary within-cluster interference and accommodate both cluster-average and individual-average target populations through general cluster-level weighting (Kahan et al., 2023). To our knowledge, this is the first effort to address interventional effect estimands in the presence of mediator spillover. Second, we derive the efficient influence functions and construct cluster-level cross-fitted estimators that accommodate flexible nuisance estimation (Chernozhukov et al., 2018). Exact bias decompositions characterize their multiple robustness properties. The estimators are consistent under the required multiple robustness conditions for the nuisance functions. And, when all nuisance estimators are consistent and the required product rate conditions hold, the estimators are asymptotically normal and semiparametrically efficient. Third, to facilitate practical implementation, we further develop a lower-dimensional reparameterization of the efficient influence function that replaces high-dimensional post-treatment confounder densities and integration over the full mediator vector with density ratios, treatment classifiers, univariate mediator densities, and conditional mean regressions. In particular, we adapt the augmented-classification approach of Rudolph et al. (2024) to estimate the key density ratio without directly modeling the corresponding high-dimensional conditional densities. We establish corresponding robustness and efficiency results under compatibility conditions on the auxiliary regressions and examine both implementations in simulation studies. We illustrate the proposed methods in the PPACT cluster-randomized trial of cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain.

2 Notation, estimands and assumptions

Consider a cluster-randomized trial with KK clusters, indexed by i∈{1,…,K}i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}. Let NiN_{i} denote the size of cluster ii, and let Ai∈{0,1}A_{i}\in\{0,1\} denote its treatment assignment, with Ai=1A_{i}=1 indicating treatment and Ai=0A_{i}=0 indicating control. All individuals in a cluster receive the same assignment. Baseline information consists of cluster-level covariates Vi∈ℝd𝐕×1V_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\bf V}\times 1} and individual-level covariates Xi​j∈ℝd𝐗×1X_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\bf X}\times 1}, for j∈{1,…,Ni}j\in\{1,\ldots,N_{i}\}. After assignment, we observe post-treatment confounders Zi​j∈ℝd𝐙×1Z_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\bf Z}\times 1}, followed by a mediator Mi​j∈ℝM_{ij}\in\mathbb{R} and an outcome Yi​j∈ℝY_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}. Zi​jZ_{ij} may be affected by treatment and may, in turn, affect both the mediators and the outcomes. Denote Zi=[Zi​1,…,Zi​Ni]T∈ℝNi×d𝐙Z_{i}=[Z_{i1},\ldots,Z_{iN_{i}}]^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times d_{\bf Z}}, Mi=[Mi​1,…,Mi​Ni]T∈ℝNi×1M_{i}=[M_{i1},\ldots,M_{iN_{i}}]^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times 1}, and Yi=[Yi​1,…,Yi​Ni]T∈ℝNi×1Y_{i}=[Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{iN_{i}}]^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times 1}. For an individual jj, Mi⁡(−j)∈ℝ(Ni−1)×1M_{i(-j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N_{i}-1)\times 1} denotes the mediators of all other individuals in the same cluster. The observed data for cluster ii are Oi={Ni,Ci,Ai,Zi,Mi,Yi}O_{i}=\{N_{i},C_{i},A_{i},Z_{i},M_{i},Y_{i}\}. We suppress the cluster index “ii" when referring to a generic cluster, using a “∙\bullet" in its place for individual-level variables; for example, we write MM and M∙jM_{\bullet j} for MiM_{i} and Mi​jM_{ij}.

Let Z∙j​(a)Z_{\bullet j}(a) denote the potential post-treatment confounders for individual jj under cluster treatment a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, and let M∙j​(a,z)M_{\bullet j}(a,z) denote the potential mediator when treatment is set to aa and the full cluster confounder vector is set to z={z∙j,z∙(−j)}z=\{z_{\bullet j},z_{\bullet(-j)}\}. Similarly, Y∙j​(a,z,m)=Y∙j​(a,z∙j,z∙(−j),m∙j,m∙(−j))Y_{\bullet j}(a,z,m)=Y_{\bullet j}(a,z_{\bullet j},z_{\bullet(-j)},m_{\bullet j},m_{\bullet(-j)}) is the potential outcome when treatment, confounders, and mediators are set to aa, zz, and m={m∙j,m∙(−j)}m=\{m_{\bullet j},m_{\bullet(-j)}\}, respectively. Dependence on the full vectors zz and mm permits an individual’s outcome to depend on both their own and other cluster members’ post-treatment variables. The potential variables are indexed only by interventions within the same cluster, thereby excluding interference across clusters.

We assume composition: Y∙j​(a,m)=Y∙j​(a,Z⁡(a),m)Y_{\bullet j}(a,m)=Y_{\bullet j}(a,Z(a),m) and M∙j​(a)=M∙j​(a,Z⁡(a))M_{\bullet j}(a)=M_{\bullet j}(a,Z(a)), where Z⁡(a)Z(a) and M⁡(a)M(a) collect the corresponding potential variables over cluster members. Thus, an intervention on the mediators leaves the post-treatment confounders at their natural values under treatment aa. We also assume Y∙j​(a)=Y∙j​(a,Z⁡(a),M⁡(a))=Y∙j​(a,Z⁡(a),M⁡(a,Z⁡(a)))Y_{\bullet j}(a)=Y_{\bullet j}(a,Z(a),M(a))=Y_{\bullet j}(a,Z(a),M(a,Z(a))), i.e., the potential outcome under treatment alone equals the potential outcome obtained by setting both post-treatment vectors to their natural values under that treatment.

To define interventional mediation effects, let G⁡(a)G(a) be a random draw from the conditional distribution of M⁡(a)M(a) given (C,N)(C,N). Conditional on (C,N)(C,N), we construct G⁡(0)G(0) and G⁡(1)G(1) to be independent of one another and of all potential variables. Each G⁡(a)G(a) is drawn as a joint cluster mediator vector, allowing the dependence among its components under treatment aa. This construction extends stochastic mediator interventions for intermediate confounding to clustered data setting (Díaz et al., 2021; Rudolph et al., 2024). Specifically, we define the interventional direct effect (IDE{\rm IDE}) and interventional indirect effect (IIE{\rm IIE}) by

IDE=h⁡(θ⁡(1,0),θ⁡(0,0)),IIE=h⁡(θ⁡(1,1),θ⁡(1,0)).{\rm IDE}=h(\theta(1,0),\theta(0,0)),\quad{\rm IIE}=h(\theta(1,1),\theta(1,0)).

where hh is a known contrast function specifying the effect scale, and

θ⁡(a,a′)=𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1NY∙j​(a,G∙j​(a′),G∙(−j)​(a′))]𝔼⁡[W],for​a,a′∈{0,1}.\theta(a,a^{\prime})=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_{\bullet j}(a,G_{\bullet j}(a^{\prime}),G_{\bullet(-j)}(a^{\prime}))\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}[W]},\qquad~{\rm for~}a,a^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}. (1)

The weight WW is a user-specified function of {N,V}\{N,V\}. As illustrated in Li et al. (2025), WW specifies how cluster-specific mean outcomes contribute to the target population mean. In particular, W=1W=1 gives equal weight to clusters, whereas W=NW=N gives weight proportional to cluster size, yielding cluster-average and individual-average interventional effect estimands, respectively. Possible scale functions include h⁡(x,y)=x/yh(x,y)=x/y and h⁡(x,y)=(x/(1−x))/(y/(1−y))h(x,y)=(x/(1-x))/(y/(1-y)), indicating risk ratio and odds ratio scales. In this paper, we focus on the mean difference scale with h⁡(x,y)=x−yh(x,y)=x-y.

In θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}), treatment is set to aa, the confounders take their natural values Z⁡(a)Z(a), and the entire mediator vector is independently drawn from its distribution under a′a^{\prime} among clusters with the same (C,N)(C,N). The IDE therefore changes treatment while holding the mediator intervention at the control distribution; it allows treatment to affect the outcome through the post-treatment confounders with the mediator draw held fixed in distribution. The IIE holds treatment at 11 and changes the joint mediator distribution from control to treatment. These effects sum to θ⁡(1,1)−θ⁡(0,0)\theta(1,1)-\theta(0,0). This sum need not equal the total effect of treatment alone. That is, even when a=a′a=a^{\prime}, the stochastic intervention breaks the natural dependence between Z⁡(a)Z(a) and M⁡(a)M(a) conditional on (C,N)(C,N). This distinction between interventional and total treatment effects is discussed by Díaz et al. (2021) and Rudolph et al. (2024).

To distinguish changes involving an individual’s own mediator from those involving the mediators of other cluster members, we further define the interventional individual mediation effect (IIME{\rm IIME}) and the interventional spillover mediation effect (ISME{\rm ISME}) as

IIME=h⁡(τ,θ⁡(1,0)),ISME=h⁡(θ⁡(1,1),τ),{\rm IIME}=h(\tau,\theta(1,0)),\quad{\rm ISME}=h(\theta(1,1),\tau),

where

τ=𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1NY∙j​(1,G∙j​(1),G∙(−j)​(0))]𝔼⁡[W].\tau=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_{\bullet j}(1,G_{\bullet j}(1),G_{\bullet(-j)}(0))\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}[W]}. (2)

For each individual jj, the intervention in τ\tau draws their own mediator from the treatment distribution and the vector of other members’ mediators from the control distribution, independently conditional on (C,N)(C,N). The parameter averages outcomes under these individual-specific interventions; it does not require a single mediator assignment to implement all of them simultaneously. Note that the IIME and ISME sum exactly to the IIE. Their interpretation also depends on the joint mediator distributions under treatment and control. Moving from θ⁡(1,0)\theta(1,0) to τ\tau changes the own-mediator marginal distribution and removes its dependence on the peer mediator vector under control. Moving from τ\tau to θ⁡(1,1)\theta(1,1) changes the peer marginal distribution and restores the dependence between own and peer mediators under treatment. Consequently, these contrasts can reflect changes in mediator dependence as well as changes in the respective marginal distributions.

Assumption (A1) links the observed post-treatment variables to their potential values, accommodating arbitrary within-cluster interference while excluding interference across clusters. Assumption (A2) specifies independent Bernoulli assignment of clusters. Assumption (A3) supplies the additional mediator-outcome exchangeability condition. Conditional on (Ci,Ni)(C_{i},N_{i}) and the natural confounder values Zi​(a)=zZ_{i}(a)=z, M⁡(a,z)M(a,z) is independent of each Y∙j​(a,z,m)Y_{\bullet j}(a,z,m). Thus, after accounting for the measured baseline information and the full post-treatment confounder vector, there does not exist remaining confounding of the joint mediator intervention and an individual’s outcome. The condition allows ZiZ_{i} to be affected by treatment and to confound the mediator-outcome relationship. In cluster-randomized trials, this differs from the sequential ignorability condition for identifying natural mediation effects in Cheng and Li (2026), which excludes treatment-induced mediator–outcome confounding. Assumption (A4) requires the clustered data are mutually independent and the cluster size is finite. It also requires positivity conditions for the mediator densities.

Section H of the Appendix describes nuisance estimation details, including an extension of the copula approach of Cheng and Li (2026) to estimate (ξ,κ,ϕ)(\xi,\kappa,\phi). 3 Identification and the nonparametric efficiency bounds

We focus on identifying θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}) and τ\tau as functionals of the observed-data distribution, based on which all interventional mediation effects are identified. The following theorem provides the core identification formulas.

Theorem 1.

Under Assumptions (A1)–(A4), θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}) is identified by

θ⁡(a,a′)=𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1N∬η∙j​(a,z,m,C,N)​ϕ​(z|a,C,N)​κ​(m|a′,C,N)​𝑑z​𝑑m]𝔼⁡[W],\theta(a,a^{\prime})=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{W}{N}\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{N}\iint\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\phi(z|a,C,N)\kappa(m|a^{\prime},C,N)\,dz\,dm\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}[W]}, (3)

for any a,a′∈{0,1}a,a^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}. Additionally, τ\tau is identified by

τ=𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1N∬η∙j​(1,z,m,C,N)​ϕ​(z|1,C,N)​κ∙j​(m∙j|1,C,N)​κ∙(−j)​(m∙(−j)|0,C,N)​𝑑z​𝑑m]𝔼⁡[W].\tau=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{W}{N}\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{N}\iint\eta_{\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi(z|1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet j}(m_{\bullet j}|1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}(m_{\bullet(-j)}|0,C,N)\,dz\,dm\right]}{{\mathbb{E}}[W]}.

 (4)

The proof is given in Section B of the Appendix. Based on the identification results for our causal targets, their efficient influence functions (EIFs) then characterize the efficiency bounds for estimating these functionals under the nonparametric model. To express the EIFs, we introduce the auxiliary functions defined in Table 1 (Panel A), which depend on the nuisance parameters (η,ξ,κ,ϕ)(\eta,\xi,\kappa,\phi).

The ratios ω(1)\omega^{(1)} and ω∙j(2)\omega_{\bullet j}^{(2)} compare the mediator distribution specified by an intervention with the observed mediator distribution conditional on treatment and ZZ. They reweight outcome residuals to the relevant intervention distribution. The functions u∙j(1)u_{\bullet j}^{(1)}–u∙j(3)u_{\bullet j}^{(3)} and r∙j(1)r_{\bullet j}^{(1)}–r∙j(4)r_{\bullet j}^{(4)} are integrated outcome regressions used to express the EIFs of θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}) and τ\tau, respectively. The next theorem gives the EIFs of θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}) and τ\tau.

Theorem 2.

The proof is provided in Section C of the Appendix. Importantly, the EIFs only depend on the observed data OO and nuisance parameters (η,ξ,κ,ϕ)(\eta,\xi,\kappa,\phi). Under the conditions of Theorem 2, the variances of 𝒟θ⁡(a,a′)\mathcal{D}_{\theta(a,a^{\prime})} and 𝒟τ\mathcal{D}_{\tau} give the nonparametric efficiency bounds per independent cluster. In the following Section 4, we establish the corresponding robustness and asymptotic results for the canonical EIF estimators directly motivated by Theorem 2.

4 The canonical EIF estimators and their asymptotic behaviors

We first consider efficient estimators of θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}) and τ\tau based on their canonical EIFs. Here, since we will use machine learning models to estimate the nuisance parameters, we leverage the cross-fitting algorithm to control the over-fitting bias associated with the nuisance estimation. Specifically, let R≥2R\geq 2 be fixed and partition the KK clusters into validation folds ℐ1,…,ℐR\mathcal{I}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{I}_{R}, with Kr=|ℐr|K_{r}=|\mathcal{I}_{r}|. For each fold r∈{1,…,R}r\in\{1,\dots,R\}, we estimate the nuisance parameters h=(η,ϕ,κ,ξ)h=(\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi) using the clusters outside ℐr\mathcal{I}_{r}, yielding h^(−r)\widehat{h}^{(-r)}. All members of a cluster remain in the same fold, so nuisance estimation excludes every observation in a validation cluster (Cheng and Li, 2026). Then, the canonical EIF estimators are given by

θ^cf​(a,a′)=K−1​∑r=1R∑i∈ℐrψθ​{a,a′;Oi;h^(−r)}ℙK​(W),τ^cf=K−1​∑r=1R∑i∈ℐrψτ​{Oi;h^(−r)}ℙK​(W),\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{cf}}(a,a^{\prime})=\frac{K^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{r}}\psi_{\theta}\{a,a^{\prime};O_{i};\widehat{h}^{(-r)}\}}{\mathbb{P}_{K}(W)},\quad\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cf}}=\frac{K^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{r}}\psi_{\tau}\{O_{i};\widehat{h}^{(-r)}\}}{\mathbb{P}_{K}(W)},

where ℙK​(f)=K−1​∑i=1Kf⁡(Oi)\mathbb{P}_{K}(f)=K^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{K}f(O_{i}).

With a slight abuse of notations, we use the subscript 00 to denote true nuisance parameters so that h0=(η0,ϕ0,κ0,ξ0)h_{0}=(\eta_{0},\phi_{0},\kappa_{0},\xi_{0}) are true values of hh aligning with the true observed data distribution. Further, let f∙jf_{\bullet j} be a generic nuisance parameter or auxiliary function with a possibly individual-specific component jj, and f∙j⋆f_{\bullet j}^{\star} be its convergent value of the cross-fitted estimator f^∙j(−r)\widehat{f}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)}, which may differ from the true value f∙j,0f_{\bullet j,0}. Theorems 8 and 9 in Section D.1 of the Appendix establish the multiple robustness conditions for the canonical EIF estimators. To describe the multiple robustness property, we use f∙j=f∙j,0f_{\bullet j}=f_{\bullet j,0} to denote the correct specification of f^∙j(−r)\widehat{f}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)} converges to f∙j,0f_{\bullet j,0} in L2​(P)L_{2}(P)-norm for every jj. Let ν0:=𝔼⁡(W)>0\nu_{0}:={\mathbb{E}}(W)>0, and NmaxN_{\rm max} denote the largest possible cluster size. For θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}), 𝔼⁡{ψθ​(a,a′,O,h)}=ν0​θ0​(a,a′){\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O;h)\}=\nu_{0}\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime}) if either (i) (η,ϕ)=(η0,ϕ0)(\eta,\phi)=(\eta_{0},\phi_{0}), (ii) (η,κ)=(η0,κ0)(\eta,\kappa)=(\eta_{0},\kappa_{0}), or (iii) (κ,ξ)=(κ0,ξ0)(\kappa,\xi)=(\kappa_{0},\xi_{0}). For τ\tau, 𝔼⁡{ψτ​(O,h)}=ν0​τ0{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\tau}(O;h)\}=\nu_{0}\tau_{0} if either (i) (κ,η)=(κ0,η0)(\kappa,\eta)=(\kappa_{0},\eta_{0}), (ii) (κ,ξ)=(κ0,ξ0)(\kappa,\xi)=(\kappa_{0},\xi_{0}), (iii) (η,ϕ,κ∙j)=(η0,ϕ0,κ0∙j)(\eta,\phi,\kappa_{\bullet j})=(\eta_{0},\phi_{0},\kappa_{0\bullet j}), or (iv) (η,ϕ,κ∙(−j))=(η0,ϕ0,κ0∙(−j))(\eta,\phi,\kappa_{\bullet(-j)})=(\eta_{0},\phi_{0},\kappa_{0\bullet(-j)}). Under L2​(P)L_{2}(P) convergence of ψθ{a,a′;∙;h^(−r)}\psi_{\theta}\{a,a^{\prime};\bullet;\widehat{h}^{(-r)}\} and ψτ​{∙;h^(−r)}\psi_{\tau}\{\bullet;\widehat{h}^{(-r)}\} to their respective limits uniformly over the fixed number of folds, θ^cf​(a,a′)\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{cf}}(a,a^{\prime}) and τ^cf\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cf}} are consistent whenever their corresponding conditions above hold at the limiting nuisance functions, even if the remaining nuisance functions are misspecified.

We need two regularity conditions for the asymptotic linearity and asymptotic normality of the canonical EIF estimators and we describe them below.

Assumption B.

The number of folds RR is fixed and Kr/K→pr∈(0,1)K_{r}/K\to p_{r}\in(0,1) for every rr.

Assumption B requires each fold to contain a nonvanishing proportion of clusters. The next assumption specifies the nuisance limits and the additional convergence conditions. To do so, we define λf,r=max1≤j≤Nmax⁡‖f^∙j(−r)−f∙j⋆‖2,P\lambda_{f,r}=\max_{1\leq j\leq N_{\max}}\|\widehat{f}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)}-f_{\bullet j}^{\star}\|_{2,P} as its estimation error compared to its convergent value under the L2​(P)L_{2}(P)-norm, where PP denotes the observed-data distribution. We further define

δη,r\displaystyle\delta_{\eta,r} =‖W​{η^(−r)−η0}‖2,P,\displaystyle=\|\sqrt{W}\{\widehat{\eta}^{(-r)}-\eta_{0}\}\|_{2,P}, δξ,r\displaystyle\delta_{\xi,r} =‖W​{ξ0ξ^(−r)−1}‖2,P,\displaystyle=\left\|\sqrt{W}\left\{\frac{\xi_{0}}{\widehat{\xi}^{(-r)}}-1\right\}\right\|_{2,P},

as the estimation errors compared to their true values, where g∈{κ,κ∙j,κ∙(−j)}g\in\{\kappa,\kappa_{\bullet j},\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}\}, and δκ∙j,r\delta_{\kappa_{\bullet j},r} and δκ∙(−j),r\delta_{\kappa_{\bullet(-j)},r} denote the errors for individual jj’s mediator distribution and the joint mediator distribution of the other cluster members, respectively.

Assumption C.

There exists a fixed measurable limit h⋆=(η⋆,ϕ⋆,κ⋆,ξ⋆)h^{\star}=(\eta^{\star},\phi^{\star},\kappa^{\star},\xi^{\star}) such that, uniformly over the fixed number of folds, max1≤r≤R⁡{λη,r+λϕ,r+λκ,r+λξ,r}=op​(1)\max_{1\leq r\leq R}\{\lambda_{\eta,r}+\lambda_{\phi,r}+\lambda_{\kappa,r}+\lambda_{\xi,r}\}=o_{p}(1). Assume 𝔼⁡{ψθ​(a,a′,O,h⋆)2}<∞{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O;h^{\star})^{2}\}<\infty, and 𝔼⁡{ψτ​(O,h⋆)2}<∞{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\tau}(O;h^{\star})^{2}\}<\infty. For each target under consideration, impose the corresponding conditions below.

  1. (i)

    For θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}), assume max1≤r≤R⁡{λη,r+λω(1),r+∑ℓ=13λu(ℓ),r}=op​(1)\max_{1\leq r\leq R}\left\{\lambda_{\eta,r}+\lambda_{\omega^{(1)},r}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\lambda_{u^{(\ell)},r}\right\}=o_{p}(1). The limit h⋆h^{\star} satisfies one of the three conditions in Theorem 8, and

    max1≤r≤R{δκ,rδη​ϕ,r+δη,rδξ,r}=op(K−1/2).\max_{1\leq r\leq R}\{\delta_{\kappa,r}\delta_{\eta\phi,r}+\delta_{\eta,r}\delta_{\xi,r}\}=o_{p}(K^{-1/2}). (8)
  2. (ii)

    For τ\tau, assume max1≤r≤R⁡{λη,r+λω(2),r+∑ℓ=14λr(ℓ),r}=op​(1)\max_{1\leq r\leq R}\left\{\lambda_{\eta,r}+\lambda_{\omega^{(2)},r}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{4}\lambda_{r^{(\ell)},r}\right\}=o_{p}(1). The limit h⋆h^{\star} satisfies one of the four conditions in Theorem 9, and

    max1≤r≤Rmax1≤j≤Nmax{(δκ∙j,r+δκ∙(−j),r)δη​ϕ,r+δκ∙j,rδκ∙(−j),r+δη,rδξ,r}=op(K−1/2).\displaystyle\max_{1\leq r\leq R}\max_{1\leq j\leq N_{\max}}\Big\{(\delta_{\kappa_{\bullet j},r}+\delta_{\kappa_{\bullet(-j)},r})\delta_{\eta\phi,r}+\delta_{\kappa_{\bullet j},r}\delta_{\kappa_{\bullet(-j)},r}+\delta_{\eta,r}\delta_{\xi,r}\Big\}=o_{p}(K^{-1/2}). (9)

Assumption C allows nuisance functions to converge to possibly misspecified limits, provided the relevant robustness condition holds. The conditions in (8) and (9), which are relevant to asymptotic linearity, concern products of errors relative to the truth and are stronger than the corresponding zero-bias conditions in Theorems 8 and 9. If one error has a nonzero limit, the paired error must converge faster for its product to be op(K−1/2)o_{p}(K^{-1/2}).

Define ψθ,can⋆​(O):=ψθ​(a,a′,O,h⋆)\psi_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O):=\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O;h^{\star}), and ψτ,can⋆​(O)=ψτ​(O,h⋆)\psi_{\tau,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O)=\psi_{\tau}(O;h^{\star}), where

Dθ,can⋆(O)=ψθ,can⋆​(O)−θ0​(a,a′)​Wν0,Dτ,can⋆(O)=ψτ,can⋆​(O)−τ0​Wν0.\displaystyle D_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O)=\frac{\psi_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O)-\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime})W}{\nu_{0}},\qquad D_{\tau,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O)=\frac{\psi_{\tau,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O)-\tau_{0}W}{\nu_{0}}.

We now state the asymptotic expansions for the two cross-fitted estimators. We assume the support and boundedness conditions stated at the beginning of Section F of the Appendix.

Theorem 3.

Under Assumptions B and C(i),

K​{θ^cf​(a,a′)−θ0​(a,a′)}=1K​∑i=1KDθ,can⋆​(Oi)+op​(1).\sqrt{K}\{\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{cf}}(a,a^{\prime})-\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime})\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}D_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O_{i})+o_{p}(1). (10)

Under Assumptions B and C(ii),

K​(τ^cf−τ0)=1K​∑i=1KDτ,can⋆​(Oi)+op​(1).\sqrt{K}(\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cf}}-\tau_{0})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}D_{\tau,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O_{i})+o_{p}(1). (11)

Consequently, the estimators converge to centered Gaussian limits with variances Σθ,can⋆=𝔼⁡{(Dθ,can⋆)2}\Sigma_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}={\mathbb{E}}\{(D_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star})^{2}\} and Στ,can⋆=𝔼⁡{(Dτ,can⋆)2}\Sigma_{\tau,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}={\mathbb{E}}\{(D_{\tau,\mathrm{can}}^{\star})^{2}\}, respectively. If h⋆=h0h^{\star}=h_{0}, the limiting EIFs are the EIFs in Theorem 2, and the corresponding variances attain nonparametric efficiency bounds.

The proof is given in Section F of the Appendix. Define D^θ,can,i=ψθ​{a,a′;Oi;h^(−r)}−θ^cf​(a,a′)​WiℙK​(W)\widehat{D}_{\theta,\mathrm{can},i}=\frac{\psi_{\theta}\{a,a^{\prime};O_{i};\widehat{h}^{(-r)}\}-\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{cf}}(a,a^{\prime})W_{i}}{\mathbb{P}_{K}(W)} and D^τ,can,i=ψτ​{Oi;h^(−r)}−τ^cf​WiℙK​(W)\widehat{D}_{\tau,\mathrm{can},i}=\frac{\psi_{\tau}\{O_{i};\widehat{h}^{(-r)}\}-\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cf}}W_{i}}{\mathbb{P}_{K}(W)}, for i∈ℐri\in\mathcal{I}_{r}. For the purpose of inference, the asymptotic variances Σθ,can⋆\Sigma_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star} and Στ,can⋆\Sigma_{\tau,\mathrm{can}}^{\star} can be estimated by the cross-fitted sample variances ℙK​(D^θ,can2)\mathbb{P}_{K}(\widehat{D}_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{2}) and ℙK​(D^τ,can2)\mathbb{P}_{K}(\widehat{D}_{\tau,\mathrm{can}}^{2}), respectively, and Wald-type confidence intervals can be constructed. Once we have θ^cf​(a,a′)\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{cf}}(a,a^{\prime}) and τ^cf\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cf}}, the interventional mediation effects can be obtained immediately.

5 Low-dimensional reparameterization and alternative efficient estimators

Recall that the canonical nuisance parameters (η,ϕ,κ,ξ)(\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi) determine the auxiliary functions ω(1)\omega^{(1)}, ω∙j(2)\omega_{\bullet j}^{(2)}, u∙j(1)u_{\bullet j}^{(1)}–u∙j(3)u_{\bullet j}^{(3)}, and r∙j(1)r_{\bullet j}^{(1)}–r∙j(4)r_{\bullet j}^{(4)}, which in turn determine the EIFs in Theorem 2. A direct implementation requires estimating conditional densities of cluster-level vectors whose dimensions increase with cluster size. Forming ratios of separately estimated densities can amplify estimation errors, particularly where the denominator density is small. Evaluating the auxiliary regressions also requires multivariate integration, which can be computationally demanding and introduces numerical approximation error when analytic expressions are unavailable. To avoid separately estimating multivariate densities and evaluating their integrals, we re-express these auxiliary functions using density ratios, treatment probabilities, univariate mediator densities, and conditional-mean regressions, similar to Cheng and Li (2026), Díaz et al. (2021), and Rudolph et al. (2024). We denote πa=πa​(1−π)1−a\pi_{a}=\pi^{a}(1-\pi)^{1-a}. Define κ∙j⋆​(m∙j∣m∙(−j),a,c,n)=fM∙j|M∙(−j),A,C,N​(m∙j∣m∙(−j),a,c,n)\kappa_{\bullet j}^{\star}(m_{\bullet j}\mid m_{\bullet(-j)},a,c,n)=f_{M_{\bullet j}\mid M_{\bullet(-j)},A,C,N}(m_{\bullet j}\mid m_{\bullet(-j)},a,c,n),

d⁡(a,z,m,c,n)=κ⁡(m∣a,c,n)ξ⁡(m∣a,z,c,n).d(a,z,m,c,n)=\frac{\kappa(m\mid a,c,n)}{\xi(m\mid a,z,c,n)}. (12)
s⁡(a∣m,c,n)=P⁡(A=a∣M=m,C=c,N=n),s(a\mid m,c,n)=P(A=a\mid M=m,C=c,N=n), (13)

and s−j(a∣m∙(−j),c,n)=P{A=a∣M∙(−j)=m∙(−j),C=c,N=n}s_{-j}(a\mid m_{\bullet(-j)},c,n)=P\{A=a\mid M_{\bullet(-j)}=m_{\bullet(-j)},C=c,N=n\}. For the spillover functional, further define

e∙j​(z,m,c,n)=d⁡(1,z,m,c,n)​κ∙j​(m∙j∣1,c,n)κ∙j⋆​(m∙j∣m∙(−j),1,c,n).e_{\bullet j}(z,m,c,n)=d(1,z,m,c,n)\frac{\kappa_{\bullet j}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,c,n)}{\kappa_{\bullet j}^{\star}(m_{\bullet j}\mid m_{\bullet(-j)},1,c,n)}. (14)
Proposition 1.

At the observed data distribution, on the common support of the relevant conditional distributions, the auxiliary density ratios in Theorem 2 satisfy

ω(1)​(a,a′,z,m,c,n)=d⁡(a,z,m,c,n)​πaπa′​s⁡(a′∣m,c,n)s⁡(a∣m,c,n).\omega^{(1)}(a,a^{\prime},z,m,c,n)=d(a,z,m,c,n)\frac{\pi_{a}}{\pi_{a^{\prime}}}\frac{s(a^{\prime}\mid m,c,n)}{s(a\mid m,c,n)}. (15)
ω∙j(2)​(1,1,0,z,m,c,n)=e∙j​(z,m,c,n)​π1−π​s−j​(0∣m∙(−j),c,n)s−j​(1∣m∙(−j),c,n).\omega_{\bullet j}^{(2)}(1,1,0,z,m,c,n)=e_{\bullet j}(z,m,c,n)\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\frac{s_{-j}(0\mid m_{\bullet(-j)},c,n)}{s_{-j}(1\mid m_{\bullet(-j)},c,n)}. (16)

For any square-integrable working outcome regression η\eta for which the following expectations exist, the associated auxiliary regressions, with the conditional distributions evaluated under the observed-data distribution, are

u∙j(1)(a,a′,z,c,n)=𝔼{η∙j(a,z,M,c,n)∣A=a′,C=c,N=n}.u_{\bullet j}^{(1)}(a,a^{\prime},z,c,n)={\mathbb{E}}\{\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,M,c,n)\mid A=a^{\prime},C=c,N=n\}. (17)
u∙j(2)(a,m,c,n)=𝔼{η∙j(a,Z,m,c,n)∣A=a,C=c,N=n}.u_{\bullet j}^{(2)}(a,m,c,n)={\mathbb{E}}\{\eta_{\bullet j}(a,Z,m,c,n)\mid A=a,C=c,N=n\}. (18)
u∙j(3)​(a,a′,c,n)=𝔼{u∙j(1)(a,a′,Z,C,N)∣A=a,C=c,N=n}=𝔼{u∙j(2)(a,M,C,N)∣A=a′,C=c,N=n}.\begin{split}u_{\bullet j}^{(3)}(a,a^{\prime},c,n)&={\mathbb{E}}\{u_{\bullet j}^{(1)}(a,a^{\prime},Z,C,N)\mid A=a,C=c,N=n\}\\ &={\mathbb{E}}\{u_{\bullet j}^{(2)}(a,M,C,N)\mid A=a^{\prime},C=c,N=n\}.\end{split} (19)

The corresponding representations of r∙j(1)r_{\bullet j}^{(1)}–r∙j(4)r_{\bullet j}^{(4)} use conditional regressions and the univariate densities κ∙j\kappa_{\bullet j} and κ∙j⋆\kappa_{\bullet j}^{\star}, as given in (20)–(23) of the Appendix. At η=η0\eta=\eta_{0}, these regressions coincide with the true auxiliary functions defined in Section 3.

The proof is given in Section G.2 of the Appendix. This reparameterization reduces the dimension of the density responses and replaces multivariate integration by conditional regression. Corresponding estimation of the nuisance and auxiliary functions is described in Section H of the Appendix. In particular, the additional ratio dd accounts for conditioning on the post-treatment confounder vector ZZ. We extend the augmented method proposed by Rudolph et al. (2024) to estimate dd from two classifiers distinguishing observed cluster records from reference copies, without separately estimating κ\kappa and ξ\xi; see Section G.1 of the Appendix for further details.

In our setting, a nuisance tuple is called compatible when its auxiliary regressions are obtained from the same working outcome regression η\eta through Proposition 1, using the true conditional distributions of ZZ and MM under the observed-data distribution. We construct θ^ld​(a,a′)\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{ld}}(a,a^{\prime}) and τ^ld\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ld}} using cluster-level cross-fitting, as in Section 4. Theorem 4 establishes multiple robustness for compatible tuples. For compatible fitted tuples, Assumptions B and D, together with the stated regularity conditions, yield root-KK asymptotic normality by Theorem 5, with the nonparametric efficiency bounds attained at the true nuisance limits. Both theorems and Assumption D are presented in Section A of the Appendix. For separately estimated auxiliary regressions converging to compatible limits, Theorem 6 identifies their additional contributions to 𝔼⁡{ψ^θ,r​(O)}−ν0​θ0​(a,a′){\mathbb{E}}\{\widehat{\psi}_{\theta,r}(O)\}-\nu_{0}\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime}) and 𝔼⁡{ψ^τ,r​(O)}−ν0​τ0{\mathbb{E}}\{\widehat{\psi}_{\tau,r}(O)\}-\nu_{0}\tau_{0}. Theorem 7 gives sufficient conditions for consistency and asymptotic normality. Both theorems, their assumptions, and the corresponding constructions are presented in Section A.3 of the Appendix, along with a discussion of the related compatibility considerations in Rudolph et al. (2024).

Panel B in Table 1 summarizes the nuisance estimation requirements and robustness and efficiency properties of the proposed EIF estimators.

6 Simulation studies

We conducted two simulation studies with shared data-generating process to examine the finite-sample performance of canonical and low-dimensional EIF estimators. The complete code for implementing the estimators and reproducing the simulation studies is available at https://github.com/daeyoungspam-stat/CRT-interventional-mediation. At each K∈{50,75,100,150}K\in\{50,75,100,150\}, we generated 2,000 independent cluster-randomized trials. The data-generating model for OiO_{i} and true values of interventional mediation effects are given in Section I.1 of the Appendix. The nuisance parameters were estimated and auxiliary functions were evaluated using five-fold cluster-level cross-fitting. Both studies used the nuisance fits specified in Table S1 of Section I.3 of the Appendix. We also applied the stabilization motivated by Cheng and Li (2026); see Appendix Section I.2 for implementation considerations including these numerical stabilization procedures and the construction of EIF-based confidence intervals. We expect the asymptotic analysis of the outcome regression stabilization described in Appendix Section I.2 (excluding the truncation discussed below) to follow arguments similar to those used to prove Propositions S1 and S2 of Cheng and Li (2026), and therefore omit the details here. We compared our EIF-based estimators to the g-computation-based plug-in method, which is calculated based on the identification formulas in Theorem 1 directly.

6.1 Simulation study for the canonical EIF estimators

The canonical study evaluated all 16 correct/incorrect combinations of (η,ϕ,κ,ξ)(\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi), denoted C-η​ϕ​κ​ξ\eta\phi\kappa\xi. The correctly specified models used the covariates and interactions listed for each nuisance in Table S1 in Section I.3 of the Appendix. The misspecification scenarios omitted baseline covariates and their interactions while considering treatment, cluster size, and the relevant mediator or post-treatment-confounder arguments. As in Appendix B of Cheng and Li (2026), the residual scale and exchangeable correlation were estimated in each training fold. We compared stabilized canonical EIF estimators using canonical parametric regression and flexible nuisance estimation. The latter supplied the same prespecified correct or misspecified feature sets to Super Learner with SL.library set to c("SL.glm","SL.ranger"). The parametric g-computation used the corresponding η,ϕ,κ\eta,\phi,\kappa fits, and exploited a 200-resample cluster bootstrap for inference.

Table S2 in Section I.3 summarizes the guarantees for point consistency, asymptotic linearity for each estimator, in accordance with Theorems 8 and 9 (see Section D.1 of the Appendix) for point consistency, and Theorem 3 for asymptotic linearity. Among the scenarios considered here, the asymptotic linearity guarantees in Table S2 apply to the theoretical canonical EIF estimators under C-1111 and to parametric g-computation under both C-1111 and C-1110.

Figures 1 and 2 display the cluster-average IDE and ISME results, respectively. Under C-1111, both canonical EIF methods remained approximately unbiased, and their performance improved as KK increased. The IDE coverage remained close to nominal, whereas the mild ISME undercoverage at smaller KK diminished as KK increased. The g-computation was also approximately unbiased with coverage close to nominal, reflecting the correct specification of its parametric models. When only η\eta was misspecified (C-0111), both EIF estimators remained approximately unbiased for IDE and ISME, as expected from the point-consistency condition requiring correct (κ,ξ)(\kappa,\xi). Their coverage was generally close to nominal at larger KK. The g-computation exhibited little IDE bias, but its ISME bias persisted as KK increased. When only ϕ\phi was misspecified (C-1011), both EIF estimators again remained approximately unbiased, now through correct (η,κ)(\eta,\kappa).

The distinction between point consistency and inference was particularly evident when κ\kappa or ξ\xi was misspecified. Under C-1101, correct (η,ϕ)(\eta,\phi) sufficed for IDE point consistency. Accordingly, both EIF estimators remained close to the IDE target and became more concentrated with KK, but their intervals undercovered, more noticeably for the parametric implementation. For ISME, the same nuisance combination did not satisfy a point-consistency condition: bias persisted, and coverage deteriorated as KK increased. Under C-1110, both IDE and ISME estimates remained unbiased, but coverage became conservative, especially for IDE.

Under C-0000, the sampling distributions narrowed with KK but remained displaced from the targets. For ISME, coverage deteriorated for all three estimators, with a substantially larger under-coverage for g-computation. The IDE coverage for the EIF estimators remained comparatively close to nominal despite persistent bias and considerably greater variation than under C-1111. We note that Figures S1–S3 in Section I.4.1 extend these comparisons to all 16 nuisance scenarios and include IIME. The individual-average results in Figures S7–S9 of Section I.4.2 show similar patterns.

6.2 Simulation study for the low-dimensional EIF estimators

To estimate the density ratio dd, we used the augmented-classification approach of Rudolph et al. (2024), adapted to clustered data. For each observed training cluster, we created random copies by replacing its mediator vector with a draw from an auxiliary distribution λ~\widetilde{\lambda}, while keeping its treatment, post-treatment confounders, baseline covariates, and cluster size unchanged. The distribution λ~\widetilde{\lambda} could depend on treatment, baseline covariates, and cluster size, but not on the post-treatment confounders. Two binary classifiers were then trained to distinguish the generated copies from the observed data, and their fitted probabilities were combined to estimate dd. We considered two constructions based on fitted arm-specific mediator means: Gaussian residual draws (G) and independent empirical residual-bootstrap draws (RB). Each mechanism was combined with glmnet, random forest (RF), or Super Learner (SL), yielding six different versions. The definition of the reference distribution and the classification-based representation of dd are provided in Section G.1. The nuisance estimation stage used the same cluster-level cross-fitting scheme as the canonical study. The working models and implementation details are provided in Section I.3.

The scenario label LD-AC denotes all-correct specification. The labels LD-T2–LD-T6 vary the specification of the nuisances for θ\theta while holding correct specification for τ\tau; LD-U2–LD-U6 reverse these roles. Table S3 in Section I.3 summarizes the scenario-specific guarantees for point consistency and asymptotic linearity, following Theorems 4 and 5, together with Theorem 7 for estimated auxiliary functions. Among these simulation scenarios, asymptotic linearity with the corresponding EIFs, and hence the corresponding interval validity, is guaranteed only under LD-AC (as in the canonical study), subject to the stated rate conditions.

Figures 3 and 4 display the cluster-average IDE and ISME results for G+SL and RB+SL under LD-AC and LD-T2–LD-T6. Under LD-AC, both estimators remained approximately centered, and their sampling distributions became more concentrated as KK increased. The ISME coverage approached nominal at larger KK, whereas IDE intervals remained mildly conservative. The two reference distributions yielded very similar centering, dispersion, and coverage throughout the displayed scenarios, indicating little sensitivity to this choice in the present Gaussian design.

Under LD-T2 and LD-T3, both effects satisfied the point-consistency conditions. The estimates remained close to their targets. Their coverage patterns nevertheless differed: LD-T2 intervals remained more conservative than those under LD-AC, whereas LD-T3 coverage was closer to nominal at larger KK, particularly for ISME. Thus, the two scenarios exhibited similar point-estimation performance but different behavior of the confidence intervals.

LD-T4 distinguished the nuisance requirements for the two effects. ISME has a point-consistency guarantee and remained close to its target, with coverage approaching nominal as KK increased. IDE also exhibited little bias and increasingly concentrated estimates, although its nuisance specification did not satisfy a point-consistency condition. Under LD-T5 and LD-T6, neither displayed effect had a point-consistency guarantee. The observed biases were modest over the examined values of KK, but the intervals remained more conservative than under LD-AC, especially for IDE.

Additional scenarios and IIME results are reported in Figures S4–S6 of Section I.4.1. These results further illustrate the effect-specific point-consistency guarantees. The individual-average results in Figures S10–S12 of Section I.4.2 showed similar patterns.

Across the six estimators under LD-AC, glmnet and RF had similar RMSE, and the SL implementations achieved comparable point-estimation performance. The SL implementations generally produced wider intervals than glmnet and RF, particularly for IDE and ISME at smaller KK. The comprehensive simulation reports can be found in Section I.4.

7 Data application: Analysis of the PPACT cluster-randomized trial

We reanalyzed the Pain Program for Active Coping and Training (PPACT) trial (DeBar et al., 2022), a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial to evaluate a primary care-based cognitive behavioral therapy intervention among adults with chronic pain receiving long-term opioid therapy. The PPACT trial comprises 850 participants within 106 primary care provider clusters, with cluster sizes ranging from 3 to 13 participants. In our mediation analysis, the outcome is pain impact at 12 months, measured using the 0–10 PEGS scale, for which higher values indicate greater pain impact. We consider the Roland–Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ) score at 6 months (range 0–1, with higher values indicating greater pain-related disability) as the mediator of interest. Satisfaction with primary care services at 6 months (range 1–5) was treated as the post-treatment confounder of the mediator–outcome relationship. We adjusted for cluster size and the following individual-level baseline covariates: sex, age, diagnosis of at least two chronic conditions, count of pain types, benzodiazepine receipt during the 6 months before randomization, baseline PEGS score, baseline RMDQ score, and average daily opioid dose during the 6 months before randomization.

We applied the five estimators described in the simulation study (Section 6) to investigate the cluster-average interventional mediation effects, including parametric g-computation, the stabilized canonical EIF estimator with parametric nuisance estimation, the stabilized canonical EIF estimator with flexible nuisance estimation, and the low-dimensional EIF estimators based on either a Gaussian reference distribution or a residual-bootstrap reference distribution. The g-computation and parametric canonical EIF estimators used generalized linear models only. For the flexible canonical estimator, the Super Learner library contained generalized linear models, elastic-net regression, and random forests; the low-dimensional estimators used the corresponding prespecified Super Learner libraries.

The mediation analysis results are shown in Figure 5. First, all five estimators indicated that the intervention reduced pain impact at 12 months. The TEs ranged from −0.54-0.54 to −0.46-0.46 PEGS points, and every 95% confidence interval excluded zero. Second, IDEs ranged from −0.27-0.27 to −0.15-0.15, which are all statistically insignificant. The indirect effects were consistently negative. For the IIEs, the g-computation and both canonical EIF intervals excluded zero, whereas the intervals from the two low-dimensional estimators were wider and included zero. Third, the decomposition effects from IIE (i.e., the IIME and ISME) suggested that the mediated pathway operated primarily through the participant’s own RMDQ score rather than through same-cluster spillover. The IIMEs ranged from −0.31-0.31 to −0.24-0.24; their confidence intervals excluded zero for g-computation and the two canonical EIF estimators but not for the low-dimensional EIF estimators. By comparison, the ISMEs were smaller and less stable, ranging from −0.12-0.12 to 0.100.10, and all intervals included zero. Taken together, the results provide evidence of a protective total effect of the intervention, which also suggests some evidence for existence of indirect effect. However, the results provide little evidence of spillover mediation through interactions with other participants in the same provider cluster. The wider intervals from the low-dimensional EIF estimators, particularly for the IIME and ISME, warrant cautious interpretation of the detailed decomposition. We remark that the low-dimensional EIF estimators also yielded wider intervals than their canonical EIF counterparts in the simulation studies, particularly for ISME (see Section I.4.1 in the Appendix).

Based on the canonical EIF estimator with machine learning nuisance estimation, we compared interventional mediation effects, which account for satisfaction with primary care services as a post-treatment confounder, with the corresponding natural mediation effects, which do not adjust for this confounder. As shown in Supplementary Table S4 in Appendix J, the estimated indirect effect, individual mediation effect, and spillover mediation effect were similar across the two analyses. However, the direct effect differed substantially. The interventional direct effect was −0.163-0.163 (95% CI: −0.426-0.426, 0.1010.101), whereas the natural direct effect was −0.277-0.277 (95% CI: −0.502-0.502, −0.052-0.052). This suggests that accounting for post-treatment confounding has little influence on the substantive conclusion regarding mediation through RMDQ but materially changes the magnitude and significance of the direct effect. Because the two analyses target different estimands, however, this difference should be interpreted descriptively and not a formal estimate of confounding bias.

8 Conclusion

We develop, to our knowledge, the first semiparametric framework for mediation analysis in cluster-randomized trials that jointly accommodates treatment-induced mediator–outcome confounding and within-cluster spillover. The central barrier is that treatment can alter common causes of the mediator and outcome, thereby hindering identification of natural mediation effects. By defining stochastic interventions on the joint within-cluster mediator distribution, we identify interventional direct and indirect effects without requiring cross-world independence assumptions and decompose the indirect effect into individual and spillover components. The proposed estimands quantify the consequences of hypothetical interventions on the joint mediator distribution and can differ from treatment effects carried through individual causal pathways, thereby providing an intervention-oriented perspective on the role of mediators that complements natural effects. For these estimands, we derive efficient influence functions and construct cluster-level cross-fitted estimators with multiple robustness properties, establishing asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency under suitable nuisance estimation conditions. A lower-dimensional reparameterization facilitates flexible nuisance estimation while reducing the burden of multivariate density estimation and integration. Extensions to multiple mediators and sensitivity analyses for residual mediator–outcome confounding merit further investigation.

Appendix B Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

Fix a,a′∈{0,1}a,a^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}. Conditional on (C,N)(C,N), G⁡(a′)G(a^{\prime}) is an independent random draw from the conditional distribution of M⁡(a′)M(a^{\prime}). Therefore, by iterated expectation, the numerator of (1) is

𝔼[WN∑j=1NY∙j{a,G(a′)}]=𝔼[WN∑j=1N∫𝔼{Y∙j(a,m)∣C,N}κ(m∣a′,C,N)dm],\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_{\bullet j}\{a,G(a^{\prime})\}\right]={\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\int{\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(a,m)\mid C,N\}\kappa(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\,dm\right],

where randomization and consistency identify the conditional distribution of M⁡(a′)M(a^{\prime}) given (C,N)(C,N) with κ(∙∣a′,C,N)\kappa(\bullet\mid a^{\prime},C,N). By the composition, Y∙j​(a,m)=Y∙j​{a,Z⁡(a),m}Y_{\bullet j}(a,m)=Y_{\bullet j}\{a,Z(a),m\}, and hence

𝔼{Y∙j(a,m)∣C,N}=∫𝔼{Y∙j(a,z,m)∣Z(a)=z,C,N}ϕ(z∣a,C,N)dz.{\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(a,m)\mid C,N\}=\int{\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(a,z,m)\mid Z(a)=z,C,N\}\phi(z\mid a,C,N)\,dz.

For each (z,m)(z,m) in the relevant support, randomization gives

𝔼{Y∙j(a,z,m)∣Z(a)=z,C,N}=𝔼{Y∙j(a,z,m)∣A=a,Z(a)=z,C,N}.\begin{split}{\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(a,z,m)\mid Z(a)=z,C,N\}={\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(a,z,m)\mid A=a,Z(a)=z,C,N\}.\end{split}

Assumption (A3) then permits conditioning on M⁡(a,z)=mM(a,z)=m, and Assumption (A1) maps the resulting counterfactual variables to their observed counterparts:

𝔼{Y∙j(a,z,m)∣A=a,Z(a)=z,C,N}\displaystyle{\displaystyle\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(a,z,m)\mid A=a,Z(a)=z,C,N\}
=𝔼{Y∙j(a,z,m)∣A=a,Z(a)=z,M(a,z)=m,C,N}\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(a,z,m)\mid A=a,Z(a)=z,M(a,z)=m,C,N\}
=𝔼⁡(Y∙j∣A=a,Z=z,M=m,C,N)=η∙j​(a,z,m,C,N).\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}(Y_{\bullet j}\mid A=a,Z=z,M=m,C,N)=\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N).

Substitution and division by 𝔼⁡(W){\mathbb{E}}(W) prove (3).

For (2), G⁡(1)G(1) and G⁡(0)G(0) are conditionally independent draws. Consequently, G∙j​(1)G_{\bullet j}(1) and G∙(−j)​(0)G_{\bullet(-j)}(0) have the product distribution with densities κ∙j(∙∣1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet j}(\bullet\mid 1,C,N) and κ∙(−j)(∙∣0,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}(\bullet\mid 0,C,N), and

𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1NY∙j​{1,G∙j​(1),G∙(−j)​(0)}]\displaystyle{\displaystyle\mathbb{E}}\left[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_{\bullet j}\{1,G_{\bullet j}(1),G_{\bullet(-j)}(0)\}\right]
=𝔼[WN∑j=1N∫𝔼{Y∙j(1,m)∣C,N}κ∙j(m∙j∣1,C,N)κ∙(−j)(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N)dm].\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\int{\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(1,m)\mid C,N\}\kappa_{\bullet j}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\,dm\Bigg].

In addition, we have

𝔼{Y∙j(1,m)∣C,N}=∫η∙j(1,z,m,C,N)ϕ(z∣1,C,N)dz.{\mathbb{E}}\{Y_{\bullet j}(1,m)\mid C,N\}=\int\eta_{\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid 1,C,N)\,dz.

Substitution and division by 𝔼⁡(W){\mathbb{E}}(W) prove (4). ∎

𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1NI⁡(A=a′)πa′​(1−π)1−a′​{u∙j(2)​(a,M,C,N)−u∙j(3)​(a,a′,C,N)}​S​(O)].{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{I(A=a^{\prime})}{\pi^{a^{\prime}}(1-\pi)^{1-a^{\prime}}}\{u_{\bullet j}^{(2)}(a,M,C,N)-u_{\bullet j}^{(3)}(a,a^{\prime},C,N)\}S(O)\Bigg].

This representation remains valid when a=a′a=a^{\prime}; in that case the two factor-specific derivatives are both present and add in the same treatment arm. Finally, differentiation of the baseline distribution ft​(c,n)f_{t}(c,n) gives

𝔼⁡[{WN​∑j=1Nu∙j(3)​(a,a′,C,N)−𝔼⁡(W)​θ​(a,a′)}​S​(O)],{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\left\{\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}u_{\bullet j}^{(3)}(a,a^{\prime},C,N)-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\theta(a,a^{\prime})\right\}S(O)\Bigg],

Combining the four derivatives shows that the influence function of the numerator is ψθ​(a,a′,O)−𝔼⁡(W)​θ​(a,a′)\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O)-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\theta(a,a^{\prime}).

For the numerator of (4), the same argument applies. Differentiation of the outcome regression and change of measure to the product intervention give

𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1NAπ​ω∙j(2)​(1,1,0,Z,M,C,N)​{Y∙j−η∙j​(1,Z,M,C,N)}​S​(O)].{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{A}{\pi}\omega_{\bullet j}^{(2)}(1,1,0,Z,M,C,N)\{Y_{\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}(1,Z,M,C,N)\}S(O)\Bigg].

Differentiation of the explicit treated-arm ZZ distribution contributes

𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1NAπ​{r∙j(1)​(1,1,0,Z,C,N)−r∙j(4)​(1,1,0,C,N)}​S​(O)].{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{A}{\pi}\{r_{\bullet j}^{(1)}(1,1,0,Z,C,N)-r_{\bullet j}^{(4)}(1,1,0,C,N)\}S(O)\Bigg].

The score of the treated-arm marginal distribution of M∙jM_{\bullet j} is represented by conditioning S⁡(O)S(O) on (A=1,M∙j,C,N)(A=1,M_{\bullet j},C,N) and then centering given (A=1,C,N)(A=1,C,N); its derivative contributes

𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1NAπ​{r∙j(2)​(1,0,M∙j,C,N)−r∙j(4)​(1,1,0,C,N)}​S​(O)].{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{A}{\pi}\{r_{\bullet j}^{(2)}(1,0,M_{\bullet j},C,N)-r_{\bullet j}^{(4)}(1,1,0,C,N)\}S(O)\Bigg].

Similarly, differentiating the control-arm marginal distribution of M∙(−j)M_{\bullet(-j)} contributes

𝔼⁡[WN​∑j=1N1−A1−π​{r∙j(3)​(1,1,M∙(−j),C,N)−r∙j(4)​(1,1,0,C,N)}​S​(O)].{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{1-A}{1-\pi}\{r_{\bullet j}^{(3)}(1,1,M_{\bullet(-j)},C,N)-r_{\bullet j}^{(4)}(1,1,0,C,N)\}S(O)\Bigg].

Differentiation of ft​(c,n)f_{t}(c,n) gives

𝔼⁡[{WN​∑j=1Nr∙j(4)​(1,1,0,C,N)−𝔼⁡(W)​τ}​S​(O)].{\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\left\{\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}r_{\bullet j}^{(4)}(1,1,0,C,N)-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\tau\right\}S(O)\Bigg].

Thus the influence function of this numerator is ψτ​(O)−𝔼​(W)​τ\psi_{\tau}(O)-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\tau.

The influence function of 𝔼⁡(W){\mathbb{E}}(W) is W−𝔼⁡(W)W-{\mathbb{E}}(W). We get

ψθ−𝔼⁡(W)​θ−θ⁡{W−𝔼⁡(W)}𝔼⁡(W)=ψθ−θ​W𝔼⁡(W)\frac{\psi_{\theta}-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\theta-\theta\{W-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\}}{{\mathbb{E}}(W)}=\frac{\psi_{\theta}-\theta W}{{\mathbb{E}}(W)}

and the analogous expression for τ\tau. ∎

Appendix D Proofs of Theorems 8 and 9

D.1 Bias decompositions

We use the subscript 00 to denote true parameter and nuisance values. For a candidate tuple (η,ϕ,κ,ξ)(\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi), the scores use the density ratios and integrated outcome regressions obtained from that tuple as defined in Section 3. The following theorem gives the exact bias decomposition for θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}).

Theorem 8.

Fix arbitrary candidate nuisance functions (η,ϕ,κ,ξ)(\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi) satisfying the support conditions in Assumption (A4), then

𝔼⁡{ψθ​(a,a′,O,η,ϕ,κ,ξ)}−𝔼⁡(W)​θ0​(a,a′)=𝔼[WN∑j=1N{∬{κ−κ0}(m∣a′,C,N)[η0∙j(a,z,m,C,N)ϕ0(z∣a,C,N)−η∙j(a,z,m,C,N)ϕ(z∣a,C,N)]dzdm+∬{η0∙j−η∙j}(a,z,m,C,N)κ(m∣a′,C,N)ϕ0(z∣a,C,N){ξ0​(m∣a,z,C,N)ξ⁡(m∣a,z,C,N)−1}dzdm}].\begin{aligned} &{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O;\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi)\}-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime})\\ &={\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Bigg\{\iint\{\kappa-\kappa_{0}\}(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\left[\eta_{0\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid a,C,N)-\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid a,C,N)\right]dz\,dm\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\iint\{\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}\}(a,z,m,C,N)\kappa(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid a,C,N)\left\{\frac{\xi_{0}(m\mid a,z,C,N)}{\xi(m\mid a,z,C,N)}-1\right\}\,dz\,dm\Bigg\}\Bigg].\end{aligned}

 (51)

Consequently, if at least one of the following conditions holds for every jj: (i) (η∙j,ϕ)=(η0∙j,ϕ0)(\eta_{\bullet j},\phi)=(\eta_{0\bullet j},\phi_{0}); (ii) (η∙j,κ)=(η0∙j,κ0)(\eta_{\bullet j},\kappa)=(\eta_{0\bullet j},\kappa_{0}) for every jj; (iii) (κ,ξ)=(κ0,ξ0)(\kappa,\xi)=(\kappa_{0},\xi_{0}). then

𝔼⁡{ψθ​(a,a′,O,η,ϕ,κ,ξ)}=𝔼⁡(W)​θ0​(a,a′).{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O;\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi)\}={\mathbb{E}}(W)\,\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime}).

For τ\tau, we establish the following bias decomposition.

Theorem 9.

Fix arbitrary candidate nuisance functions (η,ϕ,κ,ξ)(\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi) satisfying the support conditions in Assumption (A4). Then

𝔼⁡{ψτ​(O,η,ϕ,κ,ξ)}−𝔼⁡(W)​τ0=𝔼[WN∑j=1N∬{{κ∙j−κ0∙j}(m∙j∣1,C,N)κ∙(−j)(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N){η0∙j(1,z,m,C,N)ϕ0(z∣1,C,N)−η∙j(1,z,m,C,N)ϕ(z∣1,C,N)}+{κ∙(−j)−κ0∙(−j)}​(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N)​κ∙j​(m∙j∣1,C,N)​{η0∙j​(1,z,m,C,N)​ϕ0​(z∣1,C,N)−η∙j​(1,z,m,C,N)​ϕ​(z∣1,C,N)}−η0∙j​(1,z,m,C,N)​ϕ0​(z∣1,C,N)​{κ∙j−κ0∙j}​(m∙j∣1,C,N)​{κ∙(−j)−κ0∙(−j)}​(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N)+{η0∙j−η∙j}(1,z,m,C,N)κ∙j(m∙j∣1,C,N)κ∙(−j)(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N)ϕ0(z∣1,C,N){ξ0​(m∣1,z,C,N)ξ⁡(m∣1,z,C,N)−1}}dmdz].\begin{aligned} &{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\tau}(O;\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi)\}-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\tau_{0}\\ &={\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\iint\Bigg\{\{\kappa_{\bullet j}-\kappa_{0\bullet j}\}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\left\{\eta_{0\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)-\eta_{\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid 1,C,N)\right\}\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\{\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}-\kappa_{0\bullet(-j)}\}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet j}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\left\{\eta_{0\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)-\eta_{\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid 1,C,N)\right\}\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad-\eta_{0\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)\{\kappa_{\bullet j}-\kappa_{0\bullet j}\}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\{\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}-\kappa_{0\bullet(-j)}\}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\{\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}\}(1,z,m,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet j}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)\left\{\frac{\xi_{0}(m\mid 1,z,C,N)}{\xi(m\mid 1,z,C,N)}-1\right\}\Bigg\}\,dm\,dz\Bigg].\end{aligned}

 (52)

Consequently, if at least one of the following conditions holds for every jj: (i) (κ,η∙j)=(κ0,η0∙j)(\kappa,\eta_{\bullet j})=(\kappa_{0},\eta_{0\bullet j}); (ii) (κ,ξ)=(κ0,ξ0)(\kappa,\xi)=(\kappa_{0},\xi_{0}); (iii) (η∙j,ϕ,κ∙j)=(η0∙j,ϕ0,κ0∙j)(\eta_{\bullet j},\phi,\kappa_{\bullet j})=(\eta_{0\bullet j},\phi_{0},\kappa_{0\bullet j}); (iv) (η∙j,ϕ,κ∙(−j))=(η0∙j,ϕ0,κ0∙(−j))(\eta_{\bullet j},\phi,\kappa_{\bullet(-j)})=(\eta_{0\bullet j},\phi_{0},\kappa_{0\bullet(-j)}), then 𝔼⁡{ψτ​(O,η,ϕ,κ,ξ)}=𝔼⁡(W)​τ0{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\tau}(O;\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi)\}={\mathbb{E}}(W)\,\tau_{0}.

The proofs of Theorems 8 and 9 are given in Sections D.2 and D.3 of the Appendix.

Each listed combination of correct nuisance functions makes the corresponding population bias zero. For θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}), correct η\eta and ϕ\phi suffice even when both mediator density models are misspecified. For τ\tau, the product of the two mediator marginal errors remains, so correctness of η\eta and ϕ\phi alone does not generally suffice; the last two robustness conditions additionally require one of the relevant mediator marginals to be correct.

D.2 Multiple robustness of θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime})

Proof.

By iterated expectation, we have

𝔼⁡{ψθ​(a,a′,O,η,ϕ,κ,ξ)}=𝔼[WN∑j=1N{𝔼[ω(1)(a,a′,Z,M,C,N){η0∙j−η∙j}(a,Z,M,C,N)∣A=a,C,N]+∬η∙j(a,z,m,C,N)ϕ0(z∣a,C,N)κ(m∣a′,C,N)dzdm+∬η∙j(a,z,m,C,N)ϕ(z∣a,C,N)κ0(m∣a′,C,N)dzdm−∬η∙j(a,z,m,C,N)ϕ(z∣a,C,N)κ(m∣a′,C,N)dzdm}].\begin{aligned} &{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O;\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi)\}\\ &={\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Bigg\{{\mathbb{E}}\big[\omega^{(1)}(a,a^{\prime},Z,M,C,N)\{\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}\}(a,Z,M,C,N)\mid A=a,C,N\big]\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\iint\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid a,C,N)\kappa(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\,dz\,dm\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\iint\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid a,C,N)\kappa_{0}(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\,dz\,dm\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad-\iint\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid a,C,N)\kappa(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\,dz\,dm\Bigg\}\Bigg].\end{aligned}

Subtracting 𝔼⁡(W)​θ0​(a,a′){\mathbb{E}}(W)\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime}), adding and subtracting the true ratio ω0(1)\omega_{0}^{(1)}, and using

𝔼[ω0(1)(η0∙j−η∙j)∣A=a,C,N]=∬(η0∙j−η∙j)ϕ0κ0dzdm{\mathbb{E}}\big[\omega_{0}^{(1)}(\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j})\mid A=a,C,N\big]=\iint(\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j})\phi_{0}\kappa_{0}\,dz\,dm

yield

𝔼⁡{ψθ​(a,a′,O,η,ϕ,κ,ξ)}−𝔼⁡(W)​θ0​(a,a′)=𝔼[WN∑j=1N{𝔼[(ω(1)−ω0(1))(η0∙j−η∙j)(a,Z,M,C,N)∣A=a,C,N]+∬η∙j(a,z,m,C,N){ϕ0−ϕ}(z∣a,C,N){κ−κ0}(m∣a′,C,N)dzdm}].\begin{aligned} &{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O;\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi)\}-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime})\\ &={\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Bigg\{{\mathbb{E}}\big[(\omega^{(1)}-\omega_{0}^{(1)})(\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j})(a,Z,M,C,N)\mid A=a,C,N\big]\\ &\qquad\qquad+\iint\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\{\phi_{0}-\phi\}(z\mid a,C,N)\{\kappa-\kappa_{0}\}(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\,dz\,dm\Bigg\}\Bigg].\end{aligned}

Now

(ω(1)−ω0(1))​ξ0=(κ−κ0)+κ⁡(ξ0ξ−1).(\omega^{(1)}-\omega_{0}^{(1)})\xi_{0}=(\kappa-\kappa_{0})+\kappa\left(\frac{\xi_{0}}{\xi}-1\right).

Substitution and rearrangement gives the exact identity

𝔼⁡{ψθ​(a,a′,O,η,ϕ,κ,ξ)}−𝔼⁡(W)​θ0​(a,a′)=𝔼[WN∑j=1N{∬{κ−κ0}(m∣a′,C,N)[η0∙j(a,z,m,C,N)ϕ0(z∣a,C,N)−η∙j(a,z,m,C,N)ϕ(z∣a,C,N)]dzdm+∬{η0∙j−η∙j}(a,z,m,C,N)κ(m∣a′,C,N)ϕ0(z∣a,C,N){ξ0​(m∣a,z,C,N)ξ⁡(m∣a,z,C,N)−1}dzdm}].\begin{aligned} &{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\theta}(a,a^{\prime};O;\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi)\}-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime})\\ &={\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Bigg\{\iint\{\kappa-\kappa_{0}\}(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\left[\eta_{0\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid a,C,N)-\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid a,C,N)\right]\,dz\,dm\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\iint\{\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}\}(a,z,m,C,N)\kappa(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid a,C,N)\left\{\frac{\xi_{0}(m\mid a,z,C,N)}{\xi(m\mid a,z,C,N)}-1\right\}\,dz\,dm\Bigg\}\Bigg].\end{aligned}

Each of the three configurations in Theorem 8 makes both terms in (51) equal to zero, proving the theorem. ∎

Proof.

Again by iterated expectation, the conditional mean of the outcome-residual term can be expressed as

∬{η0∙j−η∙j}​(1,z,m,C,N)​κ∙j​(m∙j∣1,C,N)​κ∙(−j)​(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N)\displaystyle\iint\{\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}\}(1,z,m,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet j}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)
×ϕ0​(z∣1,C,N)​ξ0​(m∣1,z,C,N)ξ⁡(m∣1,z,C,N)​d​m​d​z.\displaystyle\times\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)\frac{\xi_{0}(m\mid 1,z,C,N)}{\xi(m\mid 1,z,C,N)}\,dm\,dz.

The conditional means of the four remaining score components are, respectively,

∬η∙j​ϕ0​κ∙j​κ∙(−j)​dm​dz,∬η∙j​ϕ​κ0∙j​κ∙(−j)​dm​dz,\displaystyle\iint\eta_{\bullet j}\phi_{0}\kappa_{\bullet j}\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}\,dm\,dz,\qquad\iint\eta_{\bullet j}\phi\kappa_{0\bullet j}\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}\,dm\,dz,
∬η∙jϕκ∙jκ0∙(−j)dmdz,−2∬η∙jϕκ∙jκ∙(−j)dmdz,\displaystyle\iint\eta_{\bullet j}\phi\kappa_{\bullet j}\kappa_{0\bullet(-j)}\,dm\,dz,\qquad-2\iint\eta_{\bullet j}\phi\kappa_{\bullet j}\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}\,dm\,dz,

where every function is evaluated at the arguments shown in (7): ϕ\phi is under arm 11, κ∙j\kappa_{\bullet j} under arm 11, and κ∙(−j)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)} under arm 00. Write ξ0/ξ=1+(ξ0/ξ−1)\xi_{0}/\xi=1+(\xi_{0}/\xi-1), subtract the true numerator, and collect terms. This yields

𝔼⁡{ψτ​(O,η,ϕ,κ,ξ)}−𝔼⁡(W)​τ0=𝔼[WN∑j=1N∬{{κ∙j−κ0∙j}(m∙j∣1,C,N)κ∙(−j)(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N){η0∙j(1,z,m,C,N)ϕ0(z∣1,C,N)−η∙j(1,z,m,C,N)ϕ(z∣1,C,N)}+{κ∙(−j)−κ0∙(−j)}​(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N)​κ∙j​(m∙j∣1,C,N)​{η0∙j​(1,z,m,C,N)​ϕ0​(z∣1,C,N)−η∙j​(1,z,m,C,N)​ϕ​(z∣1,C,N)}−η0∙j​(1,z,m,C,N)​ϕ0​(z∣1,C,N)​{κ∙j−κ0∙j}​(m∙j∣1,C,N)​{κ∙(−j)−κ0∙(−j)}​(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N)+{η0∙j−η∙j}(1,z,m,C,N)κ∙j(m∙j∣1,C,N)κ∙(−j)(m∙(−j)∣0,C,N)ϕ0(z∣1,C,N){ξ0​(m∣1,z,C,N)ξ⁡(m∣1,z,C,N)−1}}dmdz].\begin{aligned} &{\mathbb{E}}\{\psi_{\tau}(O;\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi)\}-{\mathbb{E}}(W)\tau_{0}\\ &={\mathbb{E}}\Bigg[\frac{W}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\iint\Bigg\{\{\kappa_{\bullet j}-\kappa_{0\bullet j}\}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\left\{\eta_{0\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)-\eta_{\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid 1,C,N)\right\}\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad+\{\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}-\kappa_{0\bullet(-j)}\}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet j}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\left\{\eta_{0\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)-\eta_{\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi(z\mid 1,C,N)\right\}\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad-\eta_{0\bullet j}(1,z,m,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)\{\kappa_{\bullet j}-\kappa_{0\bullet j}\}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\{\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}-\kappa_{0\bullet(-j)}\}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad+\{\eta_{0\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}\}(1,z,m,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet j}(m_{\bullet j}\mid 1,C,N)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)}(m_{\bullet(-j)}\mid 0,C,N)\phi_{0}(z\mid 1,C,N)\left\{\frac{\xi_{0}(m\mid 1,z,C,N)}{\xi(m\mid 1,z,C,N)}-1\right\}\Bigg\}\,dm\,dz\Bigg].\end{aligned}

Appendix E Generic cross-fitting machinery

The following lemma isolates the argument shared by the canonical and low-dimensional estimators. It is stated at the cluster level, so the independent sample size is KK.

Lemma 2.

Let ζ0\zeta_{0} be a generic scalar estimand, let ν0=𝔼⁡(W)∈(0,∞)\nu_{0}={\mathbb{E}}(W)\in(0,\infty), and set μ0=ν0​ζ0\mu_{0}=\nu_{0}\zeta_{0}. For r=1,…,Rr=1,\ldots,R, let ψ^r\widehat{\psi}_{r} be a random function measurable with respect to the training clusters outside ℐr\mathcal{I}_{r}, and define

μ^=∑r=1RKrK​ℙK,r​(ψ^r),ζ^=μ^ℙK​(W),\widehat{\mu}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\frac{K_{r}}{K}\mathbb{P}_{K,r}(\widehat{\psi}_{r}),\qquad\widehat{\zeta}=\frac{\widehat{\mu}}{\mathbb{P}_{K}(W)},

where ℙK,r\mathbb{P}_{K,r} is the empirical mean over ℐr\mathcal{I}_{r}. Suppose Assumption B holds and there is a fixed square-integrable function ψ⋆\psi^{\star} such that, uniformly over rr,

‖ψ^r−ψ⋆‖2,P=op​(1).\|\widehat{\psi}_{r}-\psi^{\star}\|_{2,P}=o_{p}(1). (53)
𝔼​ψ⋆=μ0.{\mathbb{E}}\psi^{\star}=\mu_{0}. (54)
|𝔼(ψ^r−ψ⋆)|=op(K−1/2).|{\mathbb{E}}(\widehat{\psi}_{r}-\psi^{\star})|=o_{p}(K^{-1/2}). (55)

Then

K​(ζ^−ζ0)=1K​∑i=1Kψ⋆​(Oi)−ζ0​Wiν0+op​(1).\sqrt{K}(\widehat{\zeta}-\zeta_{0})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{\psi^{\star}(O_{i})-\zeta_{0}W_{i}}{\nu_{0}}+o_{p}(1). (56)

Consequently, if D⋆​(O)={ψ⋆​(O)−ζ0​W}/ν0D^{\star}(O)=\{\psi^{\star}(O)-\zeta_{0}W\}/\nu_{0}, then K​(ζ^−ζ0)↝N⁡{0,𝔼⁡(D⋆2)}\sqrt{K}(\widehat{\zeta}-\zeta_{0})\rightsquigarrow N\{0,{\mathbb{E}}(D^{\star 2})\}.

If, for i∈ℐri\in\mathcal{I}_{r},

D^i=ψ^r​(Oi)−ζ^​WiℙK​(W),\widehat{D}_{i}=\frac{\widehat{\psi}_{r}(O_{i})-\widehat{\zeta}W_{i}}{\mathbb{P}_{K}(W)},

then ℙK(D^2)→p𝔼(D⋆2)\mathbb{P}_{K}(\widehat{D}^{2})\to_{p}{\mathbb{E}}(D^{\star 2}).

Proof.

Let pr=Kr/Kp_{r}=K_{r}/K. Adding and subtracting ψ⋆\psi^{\star} gives the exact numerator decomposition

μ^−μ0=(ℙK−𝔼)​ψ⋆+R1​K+R2​K,\widehat{\mu}-\mu_{0}=(\mathbb{P}_{K}-{\mathbb{E}})\psi^{\star}+R_{1K}+R_{2K}, (57)

where

R1​K=∑r=1Rpr​(ℙK,r−𝔼)​(ψ^r−ψ⋆),R2​K=∑r=1Rpr​𝔼​(ψ^r−ψ⋆).R_{1K}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}p_{r}(\mathbb{P}_{K,r}-{\mathbb{E}})(\widehat{\psi}_{r}-\psi^{\star}),\qquad R_{2K}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}p_{r}{\mathbb{E}}(\widehat{\psi}_{r}-\psi^{\star}).

For a fixed fold rr, condition on the sigma-field generated by the training clusters. The function gr=ψ^r−ψ⋆g_{r}=\widehat{\psi}_{r}-\psi^{\star} is then fixed and independent of the validation clusters, and

KVar{pr(ℙK,r−𝔼)gr∣ℱ−r}≤pr𝔼(gr2).K\,\Var\{p_{r}(\mathbb{P}_{K,r}-{\mathbb{E}})g_{r}\mid\mathcal{F}_{-r}\}\leq p_{r}{\mathbb{E}}(g_{r}^{2}).

By (53) and Chebyshev’s inequality, we obtain K​pr​(ℙK,r−𝔼)​gr=op​(1)\sqrt{K}p_{r}(\mathbb{P}_{K,r}-{\mathbb{E}})g_{r}=o_{p}(1). Since RR is fixed, we have

K​R1​K=op​(1).\sqrt{K}R_{1K}=o_{p}(1). (58)

Condition (55) similarly gives

K​R2​K=op​(1).\sqrt{K}R_{2K}=o_{p}(1). (59)

Combining (57)–(59), we get

K​(μ^−μ0)=K​(ℙK−𝔼)​ψ⋆+op​(1).\sqrt{K}(\widehat{\mu}-\mu_{0})=\sqrt{K}(\mathbb{P}_{K}-{\mathbb{E}})\psi^{\star}+o_{p}(1). (60)

Thus μ^−μ0=Op(K−1/2)\widehat{\mu}-\mu_{0}=O_{p}(K^{-1/2}). Also, ν^=ℙK​(W)\widehat{\nu}=\mathbb{P}_{K}(W) satisfies ν^−ν0=Op(K−1/2)\widehat{\nu}-\nu_{0}=O_{p}(K^{-1/2}) and ν^→pν0\widehat{\nu}\to_{p}\nu_{0}. The identity

ζ^−ζ0=(μ^−μ0)−ζ0​(ν^−ν0)ν0+(1ν^−1ν0)​{(μ^−μ0)−ζ0​(ν^−ν0)}\widehat{\zeta}-\zeta_{0}=\frac{(\widehat{\mu}-\mu_{0})-\zeta_{0}(\widehat{\nu}-\nu_{0})}{\nu_{0}}+\left(\frac{1}{\widehat{\nu}}-\frac{1}{\nu_{0}}\right)\{(\widehat{\mu}-\mu_{0})-\zeta_{0}(\widehat{\nu}-\nu_{0})\}

shows that the second term is Op​(K−1)O_{p}(K^{-1}). Substitution of (60) proves (56); the cluster-level central limit theorem concludes the Gaussian limit claim.

For variance estimation, score convergence and the same conditional Markov argument imply

1K​∑r=1R∑i∈ℐr{ψ^r​(Oi)−ψ⋆​(Oi)}2=op​(1).\frac{1}{K}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{r}}\{\widehat{\psi}_{r}(O_{i})-\psi^{\star}(O_{i})\}^{2}=o_{p}(1).

Together with ζ^→pζ0\widehat{\zeta}\to_{p}\zeta_{0}, ν^→pν0\widehat{\nu}\to_{p}\nu_{0}, and ℙK​(W2)=Op​(1)\mathbb{P}_{K}(W^{2})=O_{p}(1), this yields ℙK​{(D^−D⋆)2}=op​(1)\mathbb{P}_{K}\{(\widehat{D}-D^{\star})^{2}\}=o_{p}(1). Hence, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we obtain

|ℙK​(D^2)−ℙK​(D⋆2)|=op​(1),\left|\mathbb{P}_{K}(\widehat{D}^{2})-\mathbb{P}_{K}(D^{\star 2})\right|=o_{p}(1),

and the distribution of large numbers yields ℙK(D⋆2)→p𝔼(D⋆2)\mathbb{P}_{K}(D^{\star 2})\to_{p}{\mathbb{E}}(D^{\star 2}). ∎

Appendix F Proof of Theorem 3

We assume that the outcome-residual density ratios in (5)–(7), the auxiliary regressions entering the applicable score, and the fitted-to-true ratios that appear in the product-rate conditions below are well-defined on their corresponding supports. Moreover, we assume that there is a finite constant BB such that, with probability tending to one, the true, limiting, and fold-specific values of the outcome regressions, the outcome-residual density ratios, the auxiliary regressions entering the applicable score, and the fitted-to-true ratios in (8)–(9) are bounded in absolute value by BB.

Proof.

We verify the hypotheses of Lemma 2 separately for θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}) and τ\tau. Throughout, condition on the training clusters outside a fixed validation fold ℐr\mathcal{I}_{r}. The fold-specific nuisance functions are then fixed, while the validation clusters remain independent cluster-level observations with distribution PP.

We first compute the elementary weighted truncation step used to derive score convergence from the componentwise conditions in Assumption C. If GG is nonnegative integrable, |fr|≤B|f_{r}|\leq B, and 𝔼⁡(fr2)=op​(1){\mathbb{E}}(f_{r}^{2})=o_{p}(1), then for every L>0L>0,

𝔼⁡(G​fr2)≤L​𝔼​(fr2)+B2​𝔼​{G​I​(G>L)}.{\mathbb{E}}(Gf_{r}^{2})\leq L{\mathbb{E}}(f_{r}^{2})+B^{2}{\mathbb{E}}\{GI(G>L)\}. (61)

Letting first K→∞K\to\infty and then L→∞L\to\infty gives 𝔼⁡(G​fr2)=op​(1){\mathbb{E}}(Gf_{r}^{2})=o_{p}(1). We apply this with

G=W2​{1+1N​∑j=1NY∙j2},G=W^{2}\left\{1+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Y_{\bullet j}^{2}\right\},

which is integrable by Assumptions (A4) and C.

For θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}), set

ψ^r​(O)=ψθ​{a,a′;O;h^(−r)},ψ⋆​(O)=ψθ,can⋆​(O).\widehat{\psi}_{r}(O)=\psi_{\theta}\{a,a^{\prime};O;\widehat{h}^{(-r)}\},\qquad\psi^{\star}(O)=\psi_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}(O).

Since h⋆h^{\star} satisfies one of the configurations in Theorem 8, the exact identity (51) gives 𝔼​ψ⋆=ν0​θ0​(a,a′){\mathbb{E}}\psi^{\star}=\nu_{0}\theta_{0}(a,a^{\prime}).

We next derive score convergence. Expanding the finite cluster-level sum in (5), the difference ψ^r−ψ⋆\widehat{\psi}_{r}-\psi^{\star} is a finite sum, over at most NmaxN_{\max} indices, of terms of the following forms:

W⁡(ω^(1),(−r)−ω(1),⋆)​Y∙j,W​ω^(1),(−r)​(η^∙j(−r)−η∙j⋆),W⁡{u^∙j(ℓ),(−r)−u∙j(ℓ),⋆},W(\widehat{\omega}^{(1),(-r)}-\omega^{(1),\star})Y_{\bullet j},\quad W\widehat{\omega}^{(1),(-r)}(\widehat{\eta}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)}-\eta_{\bullet j}^{\star}),\quad W\{\widehat{u}_{\bullet j}^{(\ell),(-r)}-u_{\bullet j}^{(\ell),\star}\},

‖ψ^r−ψθ,can⋆‖2,P=op​(1)\|\widehat{\psi}_{r}-\psi_{\theta,\mathrm{can}}^{\star}\|_{2,P}=o_{p}(1) (62)

uniformly over folds. Thus the score-convergence condition in Lemma 2 is verified for the canonical θ\theta score.

It remains to verify the conditional population drift. Insert h^(−r)\widehat{h}^{(-r)} into the exact remainder (51). Fix (C,N)(C,N) and jj. For the first product in that identity, insert the true product-intervention density and apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality under the (z,m)(z,m) distribution:

|∬{κ^(−r)−κ0}​(m∣a′,C,N)​{η0∙j​ϕ0−η^∙j(−r)​ϕ^(−r)}​dz​dm|=|∬ϕ0​(z∣a,C,N)​κ0​(m∣a′,C,N)​{κ^(−r)​(m∣a′,C,N)κ0​(m∣a′,C,N)−1}​{η0∙j−η^∙j(−r)​ϕ^(−r)​(z∣a,C,N)ϕ0​(z∣a,C,N)}​dz​dm|≤[∬ϕ0​κ0​{κ^(−r)κ0−1}2​dz​dm]1/2​[∬ϕ0​κ0​{η0∙j−η^∙j(−r)​ϕ^(−r)ϕ0}2​dz​dm]1/2.\begin{aligned} &\left|\iint\{\widehat{\kappa}^{(-r)}-\kappa_{0}\}(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\left\{\eta_{0\bullet j}\phi_{0}-\widehat{\eta}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)}\widehat{\phi}^{(-r)}\right\}\,dz\,dm\right|\\ &\qquad=\left|\iint\phi_{0}(z\mid a,C,N)\kappa_{0}(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)\left\{\frac{\widehat{\kappa}^{(-r)}(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)}{\kappa_{0}(m\mid a^{\prime},C,N)}-1\right\}\left\{\eta_{0\bullet j}-\widehat{\eta}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)}\frac{\widehat{\phi}^{(-r)}(z\mid a,C,N)}{\phi_{0}(z\mid a,C,N)}\right\}\,dz\,dm\right|\\ &\qquad\leq\left[\iint\phi_{0}\kappa_{0}\left\{\frac{\widehat{\kappa}^{(-r)}}{\kappa_{0}}-1\right\}^{2}\,dz\,dm\right]^{1/2}\left[\iint\phi_{0}\kappa_{0}\left\{\eta_{0\bullet j}-\widehat{\eta}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)}\frac{\widehat{\phi}^{(-r)}}{\phi_{0}}\right\}^{2}\,dz\,dm\right]^{1/2}.\end{aligned}

Appendix G Proofs for Section 5

G.1 Augmented-classification estimation of dd

The ratio dd in (12) can also be written as

d⁡(a,z,m,c,n)=ϕ⁡(z∣a,c,n)fZ|A,M,C,N​(z∣a,m,c,n)=κ⁡(m∣a,c,n)ξ⁡(m∣a,z,c,n).d(a,z,m,c,n)=\frac{\phi(z\mid a,c,n)}{f_{Z\mid A,M,C,N}(z\mid a,m,c,n)}=\frac{\kappa(m\mid a,c,n)}{\xi(m\mid a,z,c,n)}.

Thus dd is the conditional density ratio of the distribution of ZZ given (A,C,N)(A,C,N) to the distribution of ZZ given (A,M,C,N)(A,M,C,N). We estimate this ratio using the augmented-classification method proposed by Rudolph et al. (2024), adapted to the cluster-level observed data.

For each treatment arm aa, let λa(∙∣c,n)\lambda_{a}(\bullet\mid c,n) be a user-specified reference distribution on mediator vectors of dimension nn, with support covering the support of M∣A=a,C=c,N=nM\mid A=a,C=c,N=n. The reference draw is required to be conditionally independent of ZZ given (A,C,N)(A,C,N). In a training fold, construct an augmented sample by creating, for each observed training cluster, one observed copy with label Γ=0\Gamma=0 and one reference copy with label Γ=1\Gamma=1. The observed copy keeps (Z,M,C,N,A)(Z,M,C,N,A) unchanged. The reference copy keeps (Z,C,N,A)(Z,C,N,A) unchanged but replaces MM by

M~∼λA(∙∣C,N),\widetilde{M}\sim\lambda_{A}(\bullet\mid C,N),

drawn independently of ZZ conditional on (A,C,N)(A,C,N).

Let PλP_{\lambda} denote the distribution of the augmented data. Define the two binary classification functions

ℓa​(z,m,c,n)=Pλ​(Γ=1∣A=a,Z=z,M=m,C=c,N=n),\ell_{a}(z,m,c,n)=P_{\lambda}(\Gamma=1\mid A=a,Z=z,M=m,C=c,N=n),

and

ℓaM​(m,c,n)=Pλ​(Γ=1∣A=a,M=m,C=c,N=n).\ell^{M}_{a}(m,c,n)=P_{\lambda}(\Gamma=1\mid A=a,M=m,C=c,N=n).

Then, on the common support, one has
