G.5 Proof of Theorem 5

We assume that there is a finite constant BB such that, with probability tending to one, the true, limiting, and fold-specific values of the classifier odds, dd, e∙je_{\bullet j}, η\eta, and all auxiliary regressions entering the applicable score are bounded in absolute value by BB.

Proof.

We verify the three hypotheses of Lemma 2 from the nuisance-level conditions in Assumption D. For every fold, condition on the training clusters. The fold-specific nuisance functions are then fixed and independent of a generic validation cluster.

Consider θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}). In this proof, let

ρ^r​(M,C,N)=πaπa′​s^(−r)​(a′∣M,C,N)s^(−r)​(a∣M,C,N)\widehat{\rho}_{r}(M,C,N)=\frac{\pi_{a}}{\pi_{a^{\prime}}}\frac{\widehat{s}^{(-r)}(a^{\prime}\mid M,C,N)}{\widehat{s}^{(-r)}(a\mid M,C,N)}

and define ρ⋆\rho^{\star} and ρ0\rho_{0} analogously. Boundedness and (32) imply

‖d^(−r)​ρ^r−d⋆​ρ⋆‖2,P≤B​‖d^(−r)−d⋆‖2,P+B​‖ρ^r−ρ⋆‖2,P=op​(1)\begin{split}\|\widehat{d}^{(-r)}\widehat{\rho}_{r}-d^{\star}\rho^{\star}\|_{2,P}\leq B\|\widehat{d}^{(-r)}-d^{\star}\|_{2,P}+B\|\widehat{\rho}_{r}-\rho^{\star}\|_{2,P}=o_{p}(1)\end{split}

uniformly over folds. The outcome-residual part satisfies the exact algebraic identity

d^(−r)​ρ^r​{Y∙j−η^∙j(−r)}−d⋆​ρ⋆​{Y∙j−η∙j⋆}={d^(−r)​ρ^r−d⋆​ρ⋆}​{Y∙j−η∙j⋆}−d^(−r)​ρ^r​{η^∙j(−r)−η∙j⋆}.\begin{split}&\widehat{d}^{(-r)}\widehat{\rho}_{r}\{Y_{\bullet j}-\widehat{\eta}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)}\}-d^{\star}\rho^{\star}\{Y_{\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}^{\star}\}\\ &\quad=\{\widehat{d}^{(-r)}\widehat{\rho}_{r}-d^{\star}\rho^{\star}\}\{Y_{\bullet j}-\eta_{\bullet j}^{\star}\}-\widehat{d}^{(-r)}\widehat{\rho}_{r}\{\widehat{\eta}_{\bullet j}^{(-r)}-\eta_{\bullet j}^{\star}\}.\end{split}

The remaining score difference is a bounded linear combination of

Appendix H Nuisance and auxiliary function estimation

Recall that the canonical nuisance parameters are (η,ϕ,κ,ξ)(\eta,\phi,\kappa,\xi). The ratios ω(1)\omega^{(1)} and ω∙j(2)\omega_{\bullet j}^{(2)} and the integrated outcome regressions u∙j(1)u_{\bullet j}^{(1)}–u∙j(3)u_{\bullet j}^{(3)} and r∙j(1)r_{\bullet j}^{(1)}–r∙j(4)r_{\bullet j}^{(4)} are auxiliary functions obtained from these parameters, as defined in Section 3. The conditional mean η∙j\eta_{\bullet j} can be estimated using a regression method appropriate for Y∙jY_{\bullet j}, for example, a generalized linear model or a flexible regression method such as Super Learner, with predictors (A,Z,M,C,N)(A,Z,M,C,N). Alternatively, within each treatment group A=aA=a, regress Y∙jY_{\bullet j} on (Z,M,C,N)(Z,M,C,N) to estimate η∙j​(a,z,m,c,n)\eta_{\bullet j}(a,z,m,c,n) separately for a=0,1a=0,1.

To estimate κ\kappa, first estimate the conditional distribution of each M∙jM_{\bullet j} given (A,C,N)(A,C,N). For example, following Cheng and Li (2026), specify normal conditional distributions, estimate their means by regression, and estimate their variances from the training residuals. Specify a Gaussian copula for the conditional dependence among M∙1,…,M∙NM_{\bullet 1},\ldots,M_{\bullet N}. Estimate its correlation parameters by maximizing the copula likelihood with the fitted marginal distribution functions held fixed, as described in their Appendix A.1. Evaluate κ\kappa by multiplying the fitted κ∙j\kappa_{\bullet j} over j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N and multiplying this product by the fitted copula density evaluated at the marginal distribution functions.

To estimate ξ\xi, fit the conditional distributions of M∙jM_{\bullet j} given (A,Z,C,N)(A,Z,C,N) and a Gaussian copula for their conditional dependence motivated by Cheng and Li (2026). Similarly, to estimate ϕ\phi, fit the conditional distributions of the coordinates of ZZ given (A,C,N)(A,C,N) and a Gaussian copula for their conditional dependence. For each of ξ\xi and ϕ\phi, estimate the marginal means, residual variances, and correlation parameters for the copula separately, and calculate the joint density by the same multiplication of marginal densities and the specified copula density.

We obtain κ∙j\kappa_{\bullet j} and κ∙(−j)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)} used for τ\tau by integrating the fitted κ\kappa over m∙(−j)m_{\bullet(-j)} and m∙jm_{\bullet j}, respectively. We compute the auxiliary functions by substituting the fitted η∙j\eta_{\bullet j}, ϕ\phi, κ\kappa, ξ\xi, κ∙j\kappa_{\bullet j}, and κ∙(−j)\kappa_{\bullet(-j)} into their defining ratios and integrals in Section 3.

For the low-dimensional estimator, we estimate ss by regressing AA on (M,C,N)(M,C,N) and s−js_{-j} by regressing AA on (M∙(−j),C,N)(M_{\bullet(-j)},C,N). We estimate dd using the augmented method proposed by Rudolph et al. (2024), with the two classifiers and their predictors given in Section G.1. The densities κ∙j\kappa_{\bullet j} and κ∙j⋆\kappa_{\bullet j}^{\star} have the scalar response M∙jM_{\bullet j}, conditioned on (A,C,N)(A,C,N) and (M∙(−j),A,C,N)(M_{\bullet(-j)},A,C,N), respectively; they can be fitted through conditional mean and residual-distribution models or obtained from the same fitted κ\kappa. Substitution into (14) gives e∙je_{\bullet j}. The conditional expectations in (17)–(19) and Proposition 1 specify the responses and predictors for the auxiliary regressions. These regressions estimate u(1),u(2),u(3)u^{(1)},u^{(2)},u^{(3)} and r(1),r(2),r(3),r(4)r^{(1)},r^{(2)},r^{(3)},r^{(4)} from the same fitted η\eta. Theorem 7 gives sufficient conditions on their fitted values through (33), (40), (35), and (42). For example, Table S1 records the particular fits and covariate restrictions used in our simulations.

I.2 Stabilization

Recall that ss and s−js_{-j} are the treatment probabilities defined in Section 5, whereas ℓa\ell_{a} and ℓaM\ell_{a}^{M} are the probabilities of a reference copy in the augmented sample defined in Section G.1. Throughout the study, fitted values of ss, s−js_{-j}, ℓa\ell_{a}, and ℓaM\ell_{a}^{M} were truncated to [0.025,0.975][0.025,0.975]. For the canonical estimators, fitted values of ω(1)\omega^{(1)} and ω∙j(2)\omega_{\bullet j}^{(2)} in Theorem 2 were truncated to [0.05,20][0.05,20]. For the low-dimensional estimators, fitted values of dd, the ratio κ∙j/κ∙j⋆\kappa_{\bullet j}/\kappa_{\bullet j}^{\star} in (14), and their product e∙je_{\bullet j} were truncated to [0.05,20][0.05,20]. The fitted ratios s⁡(a′∣m,c,n)/s⁡(a∣m,c,n)s(a^{\prime}\mid m,c,n)/s(a\mid m,c,n) and s−j​(0∣m∙(−j),c,n)/s−j​(1∣m∙(−j),c,n)s_{-j}(0\mid m_{\bullet(-j)},c,n)/s_{-j}(1\mid m_{\bullet(-j)},c,n) were also truncated to [0.05,20][0.05,20]. After combining these quantities according to (15) and (16), the resulting estimates of ω(1)\omega^{(1)} and ω∙j(2)\omega_{\bullet j}^{(2)} were truncated to the same interval.

We adapted the outcome-regression adjustment in Appendix A.4 of Cheng and Li (2026). Within each validation fold, separately for each θ⁡(a,a′)\theta(a,a^{\prime}), τ\tau, and choice of WW, we added a constant to the fitted outcome regression. This constant was the weighted mean of the outcome residuals, using the coefficient of the outcome residual in Theorem 2 as its weight, including Wi/NiW_{i}/N_{i}, the treatment indicator, and the inverse randomization probability. The weighted residuals after adjustment therefore summed to zero. We added the same constant to the associated auxiliary regressions: their differences in the EIF were unchanged, while the final u∙j(3)u_{\bullet j}^{(3)} or r∙j(4)r_{\bullet j}^{(4)} increased by that constant. All other nuisance fits remained fixed at their training-fold values. In our setting, the weights also account for ZZ, and the adjustment is made separately for Wi=1W_{i}=1 and Wi=NiW_{i}=N_{i}. The low-dimensional estimator uses the same adjustment with the weights represented as in Proposition 1.

Recall the estimated influence functions D^θ,can,i\widehat{D}_{\theta,\mathrm{can},i} and D^τ,can,i\widehat{D}_{\tau,\mathrm{can},i} defined after Theorem 3, and their low-dimensional counterparts defined after Theorem 5. For each method, we evaluated these influence functions using the adjusted fits. For IDE, we subtracted the influence function for θ⁡(0,0)\theta(0,0) from that for θ⁡(1,0)\theta(1,0) within each cluster. For IIME, we subtracted that for θ⁡(1,0)\theta(1,0) from that for τ\tau; for ISME, we subtracted that for τ\tau from that for θ⁡(1,1)\theta(1,1). Taking these differences before squaring retains the covariance between the estimates. The squared standard error was K−1K^{-1} times ℙK\mathbb{P}_{K} applied to the squared difference. Each reported 95% interval was centered at the corresponding estimated effect, with half-width equal to its standard error multiplied by K/(K−3)​tK−3,0.975\sqrt{K/(K-3)}\,t_{K-3,0.975}. The G-computation estimator used the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 200 cluster-bootstrap estimates.

I.3 Nuisance fitting and theoretical guarantees

Table S1 reports the exact working models used in the final simulations.

For the low-dimensional estimators, we computed u^(1)\widehat{u}^{(1)}–u^(3)\widehat{u}^{(3)} and r^(1)\widehat{r}^{(1)}–r^(4)\widehat{r}^{(4)} using exact Gaussian moments of the scenario-specific parametric outcome regression under the training-fold fits of ϕ\phi and κ\kappa. We used the full working models for ϕ\phi and ξ\xi in every low-dimensional scenario and obtained κ^\widehat{\kappa} by integrating ξ^\widehat{\xi} against ϕ^\widehat{\phi}. The applicable convergence conditions for these estimated auxiliary functions are given in Theorem 7.

Tables S2 and S3 distinguish two different claims: consistency and asymptotic linearity. P denotes point consistency of the effect estimator; AL denotes asymptotic linearity with the influence function used for variance estimation. Under a misspecification scenario, a multiple-robust P branch can hold while the product of one fixed nuisance error and one root-KK estimation error remains first order. We therefore assert AL for the cross-fitted EIF estimators only under all-correct nuisance estimation. A zero entry means that the corresponding theorem does not provide statistical guarantee for the label “1."

I.4 Additional simulation results

I.4.1 Additional cluster-average results

Figures S1–S6 report bias and coverage for all cluster-average scenarios and methods, including the IIME results omitted from Section 6.

The additional canonical scenarios show that simultaneous misspecification of two nuisances need not introduce persistent bias when a sufficient nuisance combination remains correct (Figures S1–S3). Under C-0011, both EIF implementations had small biases at the largest KK for all three effects, consistent with correct (κ,ξ)(\kappa,\xi). C-1010 showed a similar pattern through correct (η,κ)(\eta,\kappa), although its IDE intervals were more conservative than under C-1011. The g-computation showed appreciable IDE bias in both scenarios. The scenario C-1100, like C-1101 in Section 6.1, showed small EIF bias for IDE but persistent biases for IIME and ISME, reflecting the different point-consistency requirements for the direct and mediation effects.

The IIME results in Figure S2 generally followed the point-estimation patterns seen for ISME, but their coverage patterns were not identical. Under C-1100 and C-1101, both EIF implementations underestimated IIME while overestimating ISME. Nevertheless, IIME coverage remained closer to nominal than ISME coverage at larger KK, despite the lingering IIME bias. Under C-0101, C-0100, C-0001, and C-0000, the mediation-effect biases were more pronounced than under C-1100 and C-1101, and IIME coverage was poorer.

Other scenarios without a point-consistency guarantee further separate small observed bias from robustness. Under C-0110 and C-0010, the EIF estimators had relatively small IDE biases at larger KK, but their IIME and ISME biases persisted; IDE intervals were conservative in both scenarios. Under C-1001 and C-1000, appreciable biases remained for all three effects, with little separation between the two EIF implementations at the largest KK. In these two scenarios, the g-computation estimator had smaller absolute IIME bias than either EIF implementation, illustrating that the EIF estimators did not uniformly improve point estimation outside their sufficient nuisance conditions. As in the results shown in Section 6.1, increasing KK did not generally remove bias caused by misspecification.

Figures S4–S6 extend the low-dimensional comparisons to the LD-U scenarios. IDE results were unchanged across LD-AC and LD-U2–LD-U6 for each estimator since the nuisances entering IDE were unchanged. Under LD-U2 and LD-U3, IIME and ISME estimates remained close to their targets, consistent with their point-consistency guarantees. Their coverage nevertheless differed: LD-U2 tended to be more conservative, especially for the SL implementations, whereas LD-U3 coverage was closer to nominal at larger KK. Under LD-U4 and LD-U6, negative IIME biases and positive ISME biases continued as KK increased for most methods, even though coverage was often near or above nominal. LD-U5 generally had smaller mediation-effect biases than LD-U4, but, like LD-U4 and LD-U6, does not possess point-consistency guarantee for these effects.

The complete six-estimator comparison shows more variation in coverage than in bias. Under LD-T2, LD-T5, and LD-T6, the SL implementations were generally more conservative than glmnet for all three effects; RF also became conservative in several of these scenarios as KK increased. These patterns extend the SL results described in Section 6.2. The two reference distributions gave similar results for a given classifier under LD-AC and many misspecification scenarios. However, this similarity was less uniform for the mediation effects under misspecification. At the largest KK, the SL implementations had smaller absolute IIME and ISME biases under LD-U6 than glmnet and RF, whereas they had larger absolute biases under LD-T5. The G and RB versions of SL also separated more visibly for the mediation effects under LD-U5. Thus, no classifier or reference distribution was uniformly preferable across the misspecified scenarios.

Under all-correct nuisance estimation, the canonical and low-dimensional EIF estimators had similar IDE and IIME RMSE, whereas the canonical estimators had smaller RMSE for the ISME estimand. At the largest KK, low-dimensional confidence intervals were wider than the parametric canonical EIF intervals, with the largest relative difference for ISME. Within the low-dimensional methods, the SL implementations generally had the widest IDE and ISME intervals. The low-dimensional ISME coverage was closer to nominal at larger KK, while its IDE coverage was somewhat more conservative.

I.4.2 Individual-average results

For Wi=NiW_{i}=N_{i}, one can easily compute the true IDE, IIME, and ISME values of 0.4894810.489481, 0.3429650.342965, and 0.1888400.188840, respectively, based on the data geneating process given in Section I.1. Note that both the point estimator and the cluster influence function accounted for estimation of E⁡(Ni)E(N_{i}). Figures S7–S12 report the complete individual-average results. The bias and coverage patterns were broadly similar to those under cluster-average weighting; changing the target population did not materially change the comparisons among methods or scenarios.

For the canonical estimators, C-0011 and C-1010 again yielded small biases at larger KK, whereas C-1100 and C-1101 retained small IDE biases but lingering mediation-effect biases. The latter two scenarios again underestimated IIME and overestimated ISME, with IIME coverage closer to nominal than ISME coverage. The conservative IDE coverage under C-1110, C-0110, and C-0010 also persisted. Under C-0001 and C-0000, substantial mediation-effect biases and poor coverage remained as KK increased, as in the cluster-average results.

The low-dimensional estimators likewise reproduced the cluster-average patterns. IDE remained close to its target across the LD-U scenarios, whereas LD-U4 and LD-U6 produced negative IIME biases and positive ISME biases for most methods. The relatively conservative SL intervals under LD-T2, LD-T5, and LD-T6 were also evident under individual-average weighting. Under LD-AC, differences between G and RB remained small, and coverage was close to nominal at larger KK. The all-correct interval-width ordering was also similar across the two weighting schemes: low-dimensional intervals were wider than the parametric canonical EIF intervals for IDE and ISME, especially for the SL implementations, with little difference for IIME.
